selection_reason: 1) Evidence: no experiments have been run, so there is no data yet. Domain priors suggest that combining RNA and image modalities and aggregating over multiple profiles should give the highest accuracy, but how much each contributes is unknown. 2) Test: this sets a strong but moderately priced anchor. It is multimodal and multiprofile with a compact scVI (200-dim) RNA encoder, a ResNet50 image encoder, simple average-pooling aggregation and concat fusion. It checks whether the multimodal multiprofile family performs well before paying for the heavier options (transformer aggregation, ViT-L, scGPT). Later runs can then vary one factor at a time against this baseline: ablating to single-modality or single-profile, or upgrading the encoder, aggregation or fusion. 3) Why now: it targets the region most likely to hold the best configuration while avoiding the most expensive components. Expected cost is medium. Multiprofile multimodal processing costs more than the single-profile or unimodal configurations, but it is clearly cheaper than the ViT-L and transformer-aggregation variants.

1. Evidence: We have only one result. config_044 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.494 validation accuracy and 0.453 F1. That is a moderate baseline, and no design choice has been isolated yet. 2. What this tests: config_012 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else fixed. This gives a clean answer on whether a larger image representation improves accuracy. The image encoder is plausibly one of the highest-impact choices, because pretrained ViT-L features are usually much richer than ResNet50 features. 3. Why now: Answering this early tells us which image backbone to carry into later tests of aggregation (transformer vs avgpool), RNA encoder (scGPT vs PCA vs scVI) and fusion (concat vs weighted). This one-factor ablation keeps the comparison interpretable while still exploiting the multiprofile multimodal setup. Expected cost: higher than the 7.27 GPU-hour baseline, roughly 1.5–2x, because ViT-L features are larger. The potential accuracy gain and the clarity of the result justify that cost.

Evidence: with scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool and concat held fixed, the ResNet50 image encoder (0.494 acc, 0.453 F1) clearly beat ImageNet ViT-L (0.332 acc, 0.315 F1). That gap is large enough to treat ResNet50 as the stronger image encoder for now. The aggregation method is still completely untested, and it is likely one of the most influential choices in a multiprofile setup. Test: config_036 keeps the best configuration (config_044) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation, so any difference can be attributed to aggregation. Why now: a single-variable change from the current best is the clearest way to learn whether learned cross-profile attention beats mean pooling. A positive result opens a higher-accuracy branch to refine fusion and RNA encoder within the remaining 6 experiments; a negative result lets us fix avgpool and use cheaper runs afterwards. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_044's 7.27 GPU hours, roughly 8–10, because of the transformer aggregator. This is justified because aggregation is a likely major driver of accuracy.

1) Evidence so far: the best result is config_044 (scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool + concat, 0.494 accuracy / 0.453 F1). Swapping the image encoder to ViT-L dropped accuracy sharply (0.332). Swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation also lowered it (0.435). This points to ResNet50 + avgpool as the stronger backbone. Fusion strategy and RNA encoder remain completely untested. 2) This experiment changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted, on the best configuration. It isolates whether learned modality weighting improves on simple concatenation, a design choice that affects every multimodal configuration. 3) It is a low-risk exploitation of the current best setup that also resolves a key open uncertainty. The result will tell me which fusion to carry forward when I test the RNA encoder next (scGPT or PCA via config_008, config_049 or config_019). Expected cost is moderate, similar to config_044 (about 5–7 GPU hours), since weighted fusion adds little overhead to the multiprofile ResNet50 avgpool pipeline.

1) Evidence: Switching from concat to weighted fusion gave a large jump, from 0.494 to 0.713 accuracy (config_044 vs config_016). Under concat, ResNet50 beat ViT-L and avgpool beat transformer, though each of those comparisons rests on a single run. The RNA encoder is the one major design choice not yet varied: every run so far used scvi_n200. 2) Test: Keep the best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) and swap only the RNA encoder to the scGPT foundation-model embeddings. This isolates whether a richer RNA representation adds to the weighted-fusion gain. 3) Why now: This exploits the strong weighted-fusion signal while resolving the largest remaining uncertainty, with 5 experiments left to follow up, for example with pca_n2000 or transformer aggregation under weighted fusion. Expected cost is moderate, roughly similar to or slightly above config_016 (about 6–7 GPU hours), because scGPT embeddings may be somewhat larger than scVI's.

1) Evidence: weighted fusion is the clearest signal so far. With scvi_n200, ResNet50 and avgpool, switching from concat to weighted fusion raised accuracy from 0.494 to 0.713 (F1 0.695). Swapping scvi for scGPT in that same setup dropped accuracy to 0.527, so the RNA encoder matters a lot. pca_n2000 is the only RNA encoder not yet tested. ViT-L and transformer aggregation both did worse than ResNet50 and avgpool under concat fusion, so they look less promising. 2) Test: config_015 keeps the best setup (multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This isolates whether PCA features can match or beat scvi. 3) Why now: it settles the last untested level of an important design choice while staying near the known optimum. If PCA wins, the remaining 3 experiments can refine around it. If not, scvi is confirmed and later runs can check transformer aggregation or single-profile variants with weighted fusion. Expected cost is moderate, about 5–6 GPU hours, similar to config_016. The larger PCA input may add a little overhead, but it should stay cheaper than ViT-L variants.

1) Evidence: weighted fusion is the strongest lever so far. With scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool, switching from concat to weighted raised accuracy from 0.494 to 0.713 (F1 0.695). scVI also beat pca_n2000 (0.650) and scGPT (0.527) under weighted fusion. ViT-L and transformer aggregation each underperformed in one comparison. Profile setting has never been varied, since every run so far was multiprofile, so it is the largest untested design choice. 2) Test: config_013 keeps the best components (scVI, ResNet50, weighted fusion) and swaps multiprofile for singleprofile. This isolates whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed or whether a simpler single-profile model can match or beat 0.713. 3) Value: the remaining 3 experiments go best to checking this unexplored dimension first. If singleprofile is competitive, the last runs can refine cheaply around it. If it is clearly worse, multiprofile is confirmed and I can still try transformer aggregation with weighted fusion (config_025) as an extension. Expected cost is relatively low, likely about 3–5 GPU hours, below the roughly 6-hour config_016, because no multiprofile aggregation is needed.

1) Evidence: weighted fusion gave a large gain over concat. With scvi_n200, resnet50 and avgpool, accuracy rose from 0.494 to 0.713 (config_016 vs config_044). Under that best setup, scvi_n200 beat both pca_n2000 (0.650) and scgpt (0.527), resnet50 clearly beat imagenet_vit_l, and multiprofile beat singleprofile (0.537). The main untested question for the best setup is aggregation under weighted fusion. Transformer only did slightly worse than avgpool under concat (0.435 vs 0.494), and that weak concat fusion may have held it back. 2) This experiment changes only the aggregation in config_016 from avgpool to transformer. It tests whether learned cross-profile attention adds to the weighted-fusion gain. 3) It is the most direct one-change extension of the best configuration, with a realistic chance of beating 0.713. If it fails, the last two experiments can go to remaining refinements around config_016. Expected cost is moderate, about 5–6 GPU hours, similar to config_016 and config_036 and much cheaper than the pca-based runs (about 10.6 GPU hours).

1) Evidence and uncertainty: the best result is config_016 at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1, using scvi_n200 RNA, a resnet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation and weighted fusion. Three findings point back to this setup. Weighted fusion beats concat by a wide margin (0.713 vs 0.494). scvi_n200 beats pca_n2000 (0.650) and scgpt (0.527). Avgpool beats transformer aggregation (0.639 weighted, 0.435 concat). The one design choice still open under weighted fusion is the image encoder. imagenet_vit_l has been tried only once, with concat (0.332), and concat performed poorly across the board. 2) What this tests: config_034 keeps every winning component of config_016 and swaps only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l. This isolates whether a stronger pretrained image representation helps once weighted fusion can balance the two modalities. 3) Why it is the best use of the remaining budget: it is the most direct one-change extension of the best configuration and the only nearby variant with a plausible chance of exceeding 0.713. Other changes, such as pca, scgpt or transformer aggregation, have already been shown to hurt. Expected cost is moderate, about 4.5–6 GPU hours, in line with config_012 (4.49 h) and config_016 (5.90 h). That is well below the pca-based runs (10.6 h), leaving room for the final experiment.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_016 (scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Every axis we varied away from it lowered accuracy. Concat fusion dropped it to 0.49. Transformer aggregation dropped it to 0.64. ViT-L dropped it to 0.54. PCA dropped it to 0.65, and scGPT to 0.53. So the remaining untested multimodal variants (e.g., config_017 PCA+transformer, config_026 scGPT+transformer, ViT-based configs) combine changes that each hurt and are unlikely to beat 0.713. 2) Open question: we never ran a unimodal baseline. Weighted fusion beating concat so strongly (0.71 vs 0.49) hints the model gains from down-weighting the image branch. That means scVI RNA alone with avgpool multiprofile aggregation could match or exceed the multimodal best. 3) Why this is the best final experiment: it is the only option with a realistic chance of a new best. It also answers whether imaging adds value at all. Expected cost is low, likely below the roughly 5-6 GPU hours of the multimodal avgpool runs, because the image encoder is removed.

1) Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so the choice rests on priors. In multimodal cellular profiling, three choices usually matter most: combining modalities, aggregating multiple profiles per sample, and using strong pretrained encoders. 2) Test: config_051 combines all three: multimodal input, multiprofile transformer aggregation, scGPT for RNA, ImageNet ViT-L for images, and weighted fusion. It sets a high-performing reference point early. Later experiments can then remove one component at a time (avgpool instead of transformer, ResNet50 instead of ViT-L, scVI or PCA instead of scGPT, concat instead of weighted fusion, single-modality baselines) to see which parts actually drive accuracy and where cost can be cut. 3) Why now: only the best accuracy within the budget counts. Starting with the configuration most likely to be near the top makes a strong result likely early and gives a clear upper reference for judging cheaper variants. Expected relative cost is high, likely among the most expensive configurations, because of multiprofile transformer aggregation, two modalities and large ViT-L/scGPT representations. Several cheaper ablations should follow to keep total GPU hours down.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_051 (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.635 accuracy and 0.618 F1 at 2.86 GPU hours. That gives a reasonable anchor, but it says nothing yet about which design choices drive performance. 2) Test: config_049 changes only the aggregation, from transformer to avgpool, and keeps every other setting fixed. This isolates whether learned transformer aggregation over multiple profiles beats simple mean pooling. That matters because aggregation is a major driver of both accuracy and compute in the multiprofile setting. 3) Why now: a single-factor comparison against the anchor gives a clean, interpretable signal. Avgpool should also be somewhat cheaper than the transformer run (roughly 70-90% of 2.86 GPU hours). If it matches or beats the transformer, later experiments can use the cheaper aggregation when exploring encoders and fusion. If it clearly underperforms, the transformer is confirmed as the choice to keep.

Evidence: with scGPT + ViT-L + weighted fusion, avgpool aggregation scored 0.706 accuracy (F1 0.667), against 0.635 (F1 0.618) for transformer. That is a clear gap, so avgpool is the current working choice, though it rests on a single pair of runs. Fusion, RNA encoder and image encoder are all still untested. This experiment keeps the best setup and changes only fusion, from weighted to concat (config_038). It isolates how much the fusion choice matters. That tells us whether later encoder sweeps should use concat or weighted fusion. It is a low-risk extension of the best configuration with a reasonable chance of improving on it. Expected cost is about the same as config_049, roughly 2.9 GPU hours, since the architecture and representation sizes are nearly identical and concat adds negligible overhead. Cheaper ResNet50 or encoder-swap tests can follow once the best fusion is known.

1) Evidence: Weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.706 vs 0.530, with the same encoders and aggregation). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.706 vs 0.635). So the current best is config_049: scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted. The image and RNA encoder choices are still untested. 2) This experiment keeps the winning avgpool + weighted multiprofile setup and swaps only the image encoder from ViT-L to ResNet50. That isolates the effect of the image backbone. 3) The image encoder is a major untested design choice. Changing one factor gives a clean comparison. ResNet50 produces smaller image features than ViT-L, so I expect this run to cost about the same as or somewhat less than config_049's 2.9 GPU hours, well below the 7.2-hour concat run. If ResNet50 matches or beats ViT-L, later runs can use the cheaper backbone. If it loses, the remaining budget can shift to RNA encoder variants with ViT-L (config_041, config_045).

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_049 (scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Each single-factor change from it scored lower: transformer aggregation gave 0.635, concat fusion gave 0.530 at 7.18 GPU hours, and ResNet50 gave 0.632. These are single runs, so the ranking is suggestive, not settled. The RNA encoder has never been varied, so it is the largest remaining uncertainty among the multimodal design choices. 2) This run keeps the best setup (ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps scGPT for scVI-200. It tests whether a compact, task-adapted RNA latent space helps or hurts compared with scGPT embeddings. 3) Changing one factor from the current best both exploits that setup and resolves a key open question. If scVI wins, it gives a new best. If it loses, scGPT is better supported and the remaining runs can test PCA or check the modality question against image-only config_026. Expected cost is similar to or slightly below config_049 (about 2.5 to 3 GPU hours), since the RNA representation is low-dimensional and avgpool with weighted fusion is the cheap setup.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_049 (scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Single-factor changes from this setup all lowered accuracy. Transformer aggregation gave 0.635, concat fusion 0.530, ResNet50 0.632, and scVI 0.586. So avgpool, weighted fusion and ViT-L look well supported. The RNA encoder is the one key choice left open, because the PCA_n2000 option has never been tested. 2) This experiment keeps the winning setup and swaps only the RNA encoder to PCA_n2000. That isolates whether a simple, high-dimensional PCA representation can match or beat scGPT. PCA can be competitive with foundation-model embeddings in some cases. 3) It is the most informative single-variable test that still has a real chance of beating 0.706. It also completes the RNA-encoder comparison before the remaining budget goes to exploitation or to the single-profile and unimodal checks. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 3-5 GPU hours. That is similar to the other ViT-L avgpool weighted runs, possibly slightly more because the PCA input is larger, but well below the concat-fusion run.

1) Evidence: Every other axis now points one way. Within the multiprofile setting, scGPT beats scVI and PCA, ViT-L beats ResNet50, avgpool beats transformer, and weighted fusion beats concat. That makes config_049 the best so far at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. The profile setting is the main design choice still untested: all six runs were multiprofile. 2) This experiment keeps the strongest components (scGPT, ViT-L, weighted fusion) but uses a single profile with no aggregation. It tests whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps. The simplest aggregator (avgpool) beat the transformer, which hints that aggregation may add noise rather than signal. 3) It is the direct neighbour of the best configuration, so it could beat it, and it resolves the last major open design dimension before the final two experiments. Expected cost is low, likely below the roughly 2.9 GPU hours of config_049, because there is no aggregation over multiple profiles.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_049 (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Every one-factor change from it has hurt. Transformer aggregation gave 0.635, concat fusion 0.530, ResNet50 0.632, scVI 0.586, PCA 0.332 and single-profile 0.532. The near-optimum multimodal region is therefore well mapped. The unimodal baselines are untested. The RNA encoder swing (0.33 to 0.71) is much larger than the image encoder swing (0.63 to 0.71), which suggests RNA carries most of the signal. 2) Test: config_006 (RNA-only scGPT, multiprofile, avgpool) asks whether the image branch adds value or just dilutes a strong RNA signal. It keeps the winning RNA encoder and aggregation. If it matches or beats 0.706, the last experiment can refine around it. If not, it confirms multimodal weighted fusion as the best and frees the final run for a remaining variant. 3) Value: This is the most informative untested design question left. It is also cheap. Without image processing, I expect it to cost less than the ~2.9 GPU hours of config_049, probably around 1–2 GPU hours.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_049 (scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.706, F1 0.667). Changing any single component from that setup hurt. Transformer aggregation (0.635), concat fusion (0.530), the ResNet50 image encoder (0.632), single-profile input (0.532), and weaker RNA encoders (scVI 0.586, PCA 0.332) all scored lower. RNA-only reached just 0.227, so the image branch seems to carry most of the signal. The PCA result also shows that a weak RNA input can actively hurt the fused model. Untested question: how much does the image branch achieve on its own, and is scGPT actually adding value? This experiment runs ViT-L image-only with multiprofile avgpool, the best-performing aggregation, and isolates the image contribution. If it matches or beats 0.706, it gives a cheaper, stronger model. If not, it confirms the multimodal gain and points the final experiment toward refining around config_049. Why now: the other untested variants each recombine a component that has already lost to config_049, so they are less likely to win. Expected cost: moderate and lower than the multimodal runs, likely about 2 GPU hours, because there is no RNA branch or fusion.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_049 (multiprofile, scGPT, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion), with accuracy 0.706 and F1 0.667. Every single-factor change from it has already been tested, and each did worse: transformer aggregation 0.635, ResNet50 0.632, scVI 0.586, PCA 0.332, concat fusion 0.530, single-profile 0.532. The strong components are clearly scGPT, weighted fusion and multiprofile input. 2. Test: config_001 keeps those strong components and pairs ResNet50 with transformer aggregation. This checks for an interaction we have not measured. Transformer aggregation may suit ResNet50's lower-dimensional features better than ViT-L, and ResNet50 with avgpool (0.632) was already close to ViT-L with transformer (0.635). 3. Why this one: With no experiments left, we can only gain by finding something that beats 0.706. No untested neighbor is likely to do so, but this one keeps the proven scGPT, weighted and multiprofile backbone. The alternatives look weaker: scVI, PCA, concat or single-profile variants are consistently worse. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 3-4.5 GPU hours, similar to config_002 and config_051 and cheaper than the 7-hour concat and PCA runs.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design choice is uncertain. My prior is that combining modalities (multimodal) and aggregating over multiple profiles (multiprofile) are the settings most likely to reach high validation accuracy. 2. What this tests: config_004 sets a strong mid-complexity anchor. It pairs a compact scVI-200 RNA embedding with ImageNet ViT-L image features, uses simple avgpool aggregation and uses plain concat fusion. Its result gives a baseline against which later experiments can isolate single factors: single-modality ablations, transformer versus avgpool aggregation, ResNet50 versus ViT-L, the other RNA encoders and weighted fusion. 3. Why now: Starting with a likely high performer protects the best-found accuracy early. It also avoids the most expensive options, such as transformer aggregation or the large scGPT embeddings. Expected relative cost is moderate: multiprofile and multimodal processing with ViT-L features add cost, while avgpool and the 200-dimensional scVI input keep it below the transformer-based multimodal configurations.

1) Evidence: only one result exists so far. config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. That is a solid baseline, but nothing yet tells us which design choices drive it. 2) What this tests: config_041 changes only one factor, replacing avgpool with transformer aggregation. Any accuracy difference can therefore be attributed to the aggregation method. A learned, attention-based aggregation across profiles could capture differences between profiles that mean pooling averages away. 3) Why now: aggregation is a central design choice for multiprofile models and could produce one of the larger accuracy gains. Testing it against the current best baseline both exploits that baseline and resolves an important uncertainty early, which will guide later choices of encoder and fusion. Expected cost is somewhat higher than config_004, roughly 1.2–1.5x its 4.49 GPU hours (about 5.5–7 GPU hours), because of the transformer aggregation. This is justified because it is a plausible candidate for the best configuration.

1) Evidence: with everything else held fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200, ViT-L, concat fusion), avgpool aggregation reached 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Transformer aggregation reached only 0.332 accuracy. That gap is large enough to treat avgpool as the better aggregation for now and to stop spending budget on transformer variants. 2) Test: config_019 keeps the best setup and changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted. This isolates fusion strategy, an important design choice that has not been tested yet. If weighted fusion helps, it directly raises the best result. If it hurts, concat is confirmed, and later runs can vary the RNA encoder (scGPT, PCA) or image encoder (ResNet50) around a known-good base. 3) Why now: a one-factor change from the current best is low-risk exploitation that still answers a key open question, which suits a remaining budget of 7 runs. Expected cost is about the same as config_004, roughly 4.5 GPU hours, since weighted fusion adds negligible compute over concat. Cheaper ResNet50 variants can be checked afterwards to see whether similar accuracy is possible at lower cost.

1) Evidence: with scVI-n200 + ViT-L held fixed, avgpool+concat (config_004, 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1) clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.332) and weighted fusion (0.494). These are large gaps on both accuracy and F1, so avgpool+concat looks like the right aggregation and fusion choice. The main untested uncertainty is now the encoders, and the RNA encoder is a key design choice. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) and swaps scVI-n200 for scGPT. That isolates whether a foundation-model RNA embedding improves on scVI. 3) It is a one-factor change on the current best configuration, so the result is easy to interpret. It could produce a new best, and it tells us whether later experiments should stay with scVI or move to scGPT, or go on to test PCA or ResNet50. Expected cost is similar to the earlier multiprofile ViT-L runs, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, possibly slightly more if the scGPT embeddings are larger.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_004 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Changing one factor from it hurt every time. Transformer aggregation dropped to 0.33, weighted fusion to 0.49, and scGPT to 0.23. So avgpool, concat and scVI look like the strongest choices for now. The image encoder has never been varied, which makes it the largest untested factor near the best configuration. 2) Test: config_025 keeps config_004 and swaps only ViT-L for ResNet50. This shows whether the image backbone matters, and whether a smaller CNN embedding generalises as well or better. 3) Why now: it is a controlled one-factor step next to the current best, so it can either beat it or settle the image-encoder choice for the remaining budget. Swapping PCA for scVI is the natural follow-up. Expected cost is lower than config_004's 4.49 GPU hours, roughly 3–4, because ResNet50 features are smaller and cheaper to process than ViT-L.

1) Evidence: config_004 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) is clearly best at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Each single-axis change from it has hurt badly: transformer aggregation gave 0.33, weighted fusion 0.49, the scGPT encoder 0.23 and ResNet50 0.43. 2) Test: config_002 keeps the winning setup and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. That is the last untested RNA encoder, and the RNA representation has shown the largest effect so far (scvi 0.72 vs scGPT 0.23). The result shows whether a simpler, higher-dimensional PCA input can match or beat scVI. 3) Why now: this is a clean one-variable step from the best configuration and the most likely remaining way to improve on it. The other options left are the singleprofile setting and unimodal ablations. Expected cost is moderate and similar to config_004, about 4.5–5 GPU hours. PCA features may be slightly cheaper than learned encoders, and the run should be well below the roughly 7 GPU hours of the scGPT and ResNet50 runs.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_004 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Changing one component at a time from it always hurt: transformer aggregation (0.33), weighted fusion (0.49), scGPT (0.23), ResNet50 (0.43) and PCA (0.62). That makes scVI, ViT-L, avgpool and concat the likely best choices on each axis already tested. The profile setting is the one major design choice never tested, since every run so far was multiprofile. 2) Question: config_051 keeps config_004's winning components and switches only to singleprofile. It tests whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps, or whether a simpler per-profile model generalizes better. 3) Why now: This is the largest remaining source of uncertainty and the only clear path left to beat 0.725. Refining components further looks unlikely to pay off given the consistent drops. Expected cost is lower than the roughly 4.5 GPU hours of config_004, because singleprofile training skips aggregating over multiple profiles. The result will also tell us whether the last two experiments should explore singleprofile variants or confirm the multiprofile setup.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_004 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat, acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Every single-factor change from it has now been tested, and all were clearly worse: transformer aggregation (0.33), weighted fusion (0.49), scGPT (0.23), PCA (0.62), ResNet50 (0.43) and single-profile (0.52). The RNA encoder choice caused the largest swings (scVI far ahead of PCA and scGPT), which suggests the scVI RNA representation carries much of the signal. The one major design choice still untested near the optimum is modality. This experiment: RNA-only with scVI, multiprofile and avgpool, keeping the winning RNA and aggregation settings. It tests whether the image branch adds information or partly adds noise under concat fusion. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.725, the final experiment can refine around RNA-only. If not, it confirms that multimodal fusion is needed and points the last run toward an image-only or fusion check. Why now: with two runs left, this ablation is the most informative untested step that still has a plausible chance of a new best. Expected cost: lower than the ~4.5 GPU-hour multimodal ViT-L runs, likely around 1–3 GPU hours, because the large image encoder is not used.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.725 accuracy. Every single-factor change from it scored lower: transformer aggregation 0.33, weighted fusion 0.49, scGPT 0.23, ResNet50 0.43, PCA 0.62 and single-profile 0.52. RNA-only reached just 0.21, so most of the signal seems to come from the ViT-L image features. The main untested design choice is whether the RNA branch helps or only adds noise. 2) Test: config_012 is image-only, multiprofile, ViT-L with avgpool. It isolates the image contribution while keeping the components that worked best. If it matches or beats 0.725, RNA fusion is unnecessary and this becomes the best and simplest model. If it falls short, that confirms multimodal concat adds value. 3) Why this is the best use of the budget: most other remaining options combine choices that already underperformed (transformer, weighted, scGPT, ResNet). This is the most plausible remaining candidate to beat the incumbent. Expected cost is moderate, likely somewhat below the roughly 4.5 GPU hours of the multimodal ViT-L avgpool runs because there is no RNA branch or fusion.

1) Evidence: the best result is config_004 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.725 accuracy. Every single-factor change from it lowered accuracy: transformer aggregation 0.33, weighted fusion 0.49, ResNet50 0.43, scGPT 0.23, PCA 0.62 and single-profile 0.52. So no remaining untested configuration is clearly likely to beat 0.725. 2) Test: config_028 checks whether the PCA encoder (second-best RNA encoder) with ViT-L and concat fusion holds up in the cheaper single-profile setting. 1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence on any design axis: modality, single vs. multiple profiles, encoder, aggregation or fusion. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_050 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat; acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Weighted fusion is about equal (0.715, with a slightly higher F1). 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_050 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.725 accuracy. Each change from it has lowered accuracy. 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile model with scvi_n200, resnet50, a transformer aggregator and concat fusion reached 0.573 accuracy and 0.573 F1. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_006 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + concat, 0.635 acc, 0.618 F1). Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.520 vs 0.619 for scGPT). 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_006 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.635 accuracy and 0.618 F1. Several design choices look settled. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, transformer, concat) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. The search shows clear trends. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool by a wide margin (0.706 vs 0.471). Concat fusion beats weighted fusion (0.706 vs 0.619). scVI is the strongest RNA encoder, ahead of PCA (0.650) and scGPT (0.632). ViT-L is slightly ahead of ResNet50 (0.706 vs 0.688). RNA-only reaches just 0.26, so image features appear to carry most of the signal. Most untested neighbours of config_024 only swap in components that have already lost (weighted fusion, avgpool, weaker encoders, single-profile), so they are unlikely to beat it. The main open question is how much the RNA branch actually adds. 2) This experiment: config_005 runs the winning image setup (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer) without RNA. It tells us whether RNA fusion gives a real gain or adds noise. Image-only could plausibly match or beat the multimodal model, given how weak RNA is alone and how sensitive performance is to the RNA encoder choice. 3) Why now: it is the remaining configuration most likely to beat 0.706 that has not already been ruled out by earlier results. Its outcome will guide the last two experiments. Expected cost is lower than the multimodal runs, likely about 3–4 GPU hours, since the RNA branch and fusion are removed.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_024 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Every single-factor deviation from it scored lower. Swapping to ResNet50 gave 0.688. Swapping the RNA encoder to PCA gave 0.650 and to scGPT 0.632. Weighted fusion gave 0.619, and avgpool aggregation gave 0.471. As a result, the remaining multiprofile variants (e.g., config_020, config_045, config_007) each combine at least one factor already seen to hurt, so they are unlikely to beat 0.706. 2) The single-profile setting is the one major design dimension still untested. config_026 keeps the best encoder and fusion choices (scVI, ViT-L, concat) and tests whether skipping multiprofile aggregation helps. The large avgpool penalty shows the aggregation step matters a lot, so a single-profile model could plausibly be competitive, but this is genuinely uncertain. 3) With one experiment left after this, it is the only remaining candidate with a realistic chance of a new best. It also reduces uncertainty about the profile setting. Expected cost is lower than the multiprofile runs, roughly 2–3 GPU hours versus about 4.5, since there is no multiprofile aggregation.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_024 at 0.706 accuracy (scVI + ViT-L, multimodal multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion). Four design choices clearly matter. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.47). Concat fusion beats weighted (0.62). Multiprofile beats singleprofile (0.23). Multimodal beats either modality alone. Swapping in ResNet50 for ViT-L lost very little (0.688 vs 0.706). Among RNA encoders, scVI beat PCA, and PCA beat scGPT. 2. What this tests: The untested configurations closest to the best recipe each change one remaining choice. Weighted fusion (config_020) and scGPT (config_007) carried larger penalties than PCA. PCA + ResNet50 under the winning transformer + concat recipe (config_045) therefore has the highest expected accuracy. It also tests whether PCA features pair better with a CNN image encoder than with ViT-L, an interaction that could push past 0.706. 3. Why this use of the final experiment: Only the best accuracy counts, and config_045 keeps every component of the strongest structural recipe. It probes the one remaining interaction with a realistic chance of an upside. Expected cost is moderate, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, similar to the other multimodal transformer runs.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so the main design choices are all open. These are modality (multimodal vs single), profile setting (multiprofile vs single), aggregation, encoders and fusion. Domain priors suggest that combining RNA and image data, and aggregating several profiles per sample, are the choices most likely to give the highest accuracy. 2. What this tests: config_001 combines both of those choices (multiprofile, transformer aggregation) but uses the cheaper encoders: scVI-200 for RNA, ResNet50 for images, and simple concat fusion. It tests whether that likely-best structure is strong before we pay for larger encoders. It also gives a central reference point. Later runs can change one factor at a time against it: avgpool vs transformer, ResNet50 vs ViT-L, scVI vs scGPT, concat vs weighted, and single-modality ablations. 3. Why it is the best first experiment: It puts a high-potential configuration on the board early while avoiding the most expensive options (ViT-L and scGPT). Expected cost is medium to high. Multiprofile transformer aggregation over two modalities costs more than singleprofile or unimodal runs, but should cost well under half of the ViT-L/scGPT multiprofile variants.

1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile setup (scVI RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.537 accuracy and 0.518 F1. That is a moderate baseline, and every design choice is still open. 2. Test: config_030 keeps everything the same except the image encoder, swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This is a clean single-variable test of a choice that is likely to matter a lot, because a larger pretrained backbone often gives much richer morphology features. 3. Why now: if ViT-L helps clearly, the remaining 8 experiments can build on it by varying the RNA encoder, fusion and aggregation. If it does not help, we can stay with the cheaper ResNet50 and look elsewhere. Expected cost is higher than config_001, roughly 1.5–2x (about 8–10 GPU hours), because of the larger image representations. I accept that because the image encoder is plausibly the biggest lever on accuracy.

1) Evidence: The two completed runs differ only in the image encoder. Swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l raised accuracy from 0.537 to 0.725, and F1 rose with it (0.518 to 0.685). This is a large gap, so ViT-L is clearly the image encoder to build on. The RNA encoder, fusion and aggregation choices are still untested. 2) Test: Keep the best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and change only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scGPT, a pretrained foundation model. This shows whether a richer RNA representation adds accuracy on top of the strong image features. 3) Why now: Changing one factor at a time builds directly on the best result while answering a key open design question. That leaves 6 runs to test fusion (weighted), aggregation (avgpool) and an image-only check. Expected cost is similar to config_030 (~4.5-5.5 GPU hours), possibly slightly higher because scGPT embeddings are larger.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder has had the largest effect so far. With imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation and concat fusion held fixed, scvi_n200 scored 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1, while scgpt scored only 0.435. The image encoder also matters: vit_l clearly beat resnet50 (0.537). The remaining RNA option, pca_n2000, is untested and is the biggest open question. 2) Test: config_036 keeps the best setup (vit_l, multiprofile, transformer, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This shows whether a simple high-dimensional PCA representation can match or beat scVI, which tells us which RNA backbone to refine with fusion and aggregation changes in the remaining 5 experiments. 3) Value: Changing one factor on a component with a large measured effect gives the most informative result, and it could directly produce a new best. Expected cost is similar to config_030, about 4.5-5.5 GPU hours (multiprofile, multimodal, transformer, vit_l). The larger 2000-dimensional PCA input may add a little cost but should not change it much.

1) Evidence: ImageNet ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50 as the image encoder (0.725 vs 0.537 with scVI). Among RNA encoders, scVI (0.725) is ahead of PCA (0.688), and scGPT performs poorly (0.435). Every run so far used transformer aggregation with concat fusion, so fusion and aggregation are both still untested. 2) This run keeps the best setup (scVI, ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer) and changes only fusion from concat to weighted. That isolates the effect of fusion on the strongest backbone, and a positive result would directly set a new best. 3) Fusion is a core multimodal design choice that has not been explored at all, so testing it on the leading configuration offers both exploitation and uncertainty reduction. The avgpool aggregation variant can follow next as a cheaper ablation. Expected cost is similar to config_030, roughly 4.5-5 GPU hours, since weighted fusion adds negligible overhead.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_030 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer, concat) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50 (0.725 vs 0.537). scVI beats PCA (0.688), and scGPT is far behind (0.435). Concat beats weighted fusion (0.632). Every run so far used transformer aggregation, so aggregation is the main untested choice next to the best configuration. 2. Test: config_011 keeps all of config_030's winning settings and swaps transformer aggregation for avgpool. This shows whether the transformer aggregator is needed or whether a simpler pooling does as well or better. 3. Why now: it exploits the best direction while settling the last uncertain design choice in that region, which will guide the remaining 3 experiments. Expected cost: likely a bit cheaper than config_030 (about 4 GPU hours or less), since avgpool is lighter than a transformer aggregator.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_030 (scVI-200 + ViT-L + transformer aggregation + concat fusion), at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Every single change from it has lowered accuracy: weighted fusion gave 0.632, avgpool 0.639, PCA-2000 0.688, ResNet50 0.537 and scGPT 0.435. The largest open question is how much the RNA branch actually contributes. The collapse with scGPT shows a weak RNA encoder can strongly hurt the fused model, so the image branch alone may carry most of the signal. 2) This experiment: config_049 is image-only ViT-L with transformer aggregation over multiple profiles, which is config_030 with the RNA branch removed. If it matches or beats 0.725, multimodality is not helping and later runs should focus on the image side. If it falls well short, scVI-200 RNA is adding real value and the last runs should refine multimodal variants around config_030, such as single-profile or PCA alternatives. 3) Why now: the modality question has the biggest unexplored effect, and the result directly shapes the remaining 2 experiments. It also has a realistic chance of a new best. Expected cost is lower than the ~4.6 GPU-hour multimodal ViT-L transformer runs, likely around 3–4 GPU hours, because there is no RNA encoder or fusion step.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is multiprofile scVI + ViT-L with transformer aggregation and concat fusion (config_030, 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1). ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50 (0.725 vs 0.537). scVI beats PCA (0.688) and scGPT (0.435). Concat beats weighted fusion (0.632), and transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.639). Image-only multiprofile ViT reaches 0.713 at only 1.44 GPU hours, so RNA currently adds only about one point. The largest untested design axis is profile setting: every run so far has been multiprofile. 2) This experiment keeps the best encoders and fusion (scVI + ViT-L, concat) and switches to singleprofile, which has no aggregation step. It tests whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed. Singleprofile models might also do better, since they avoid noise from aggregating many profiles. 3) Most remaining multiprofile variants change components that have already been shown to be worse, so they are unlikely to beat 0.725. This run resolves the one major remaining uncertainty with a plausible chance of a new best. If it helps, the last two experiments can exploit singleprofile variants. Expected cost is lower than the multiprofile multimodal runs (roughly 2–3 GPU hours versus about 4.5), because there is no multiprofile transformer aggregation.

1) Evidence: imagenet_vit_l is the dominant factor. Every strong run uses it, and the best result so far is config_030 (scvi_n200 + vit_l, multiprofile transformer, concat) at 0.725 accuracy. Swapping in scgpt or resnet50, or using weighted fusion or avgpool, clearly hurts. Image-only multiprofile (config_049, 0.713 accuracy, 1.44 GPU hours) nearly matches the best and has the highest F1 (0.695). Single-profile multimodal (config_040, 0.715 accuracy, 0.62 GPU hours) is also close at a fraction of the cost. So the RNA branch and the multiprofile aggregation each seem to add little on top of vit_l. 2) This run tests image-only vit_l in single-profile mode, the simplest untested variant of the strong backbone. It isolates whether RNA fusion and profile aggregation matter at all, and it could match or exceed the top accuracy without either. 3) Why now: the remaining multimodal variants mostly re-use settings already shown to hurt (weighted fusion, avgpool, pca or scgpt encoders), so they are unlikely to beat 0.725. This run is the cheapest in the space (expected about 0.3–0.6 GPU hours, below config_040). It resolves a key design question cheaply and keeps the final experiment free for the best follow-up.

1. Evidence: the best result is config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, concat) at 0.725 accuracy. The single-profile version, config_040, nearly matches it (0.715 accuracy, 0.687 F1) at about one-seventh of the cost. Image-only single-profile reaches only 0.494, so the RNA modality carries most of the signal at single-profile level. Concat fusion clearly beat weighted (by about 0.09) and transformer beat avgpool (by about 0.09), so options using weighted fusion or avgpool look unlikely to win. PCA_n2000 was only modestly behind scVI in the multiprofile setting (0.688 vs 0.725), and scGPT was poor. 2. Test: this run asks whether the richer pca_n2000 RNA representation beats scVI in the single-profile ViT-L concat setup. Without multiprofile aggregation, raw gene-level variance may matter more, so it could exceed 0.725. 3. Why this run: as the final experiment, it keeps every component that has worked well (ViT-L, concat fusion, the strong single-profile multimodal setup) and varies only the remaining plausible lever. The alternatives depend on choices already shown to underperform. Expected cost is low, about 0.6–0.8 GPU hours, similar to config_040 and far below the roughly 4–5 GPU hours of the multiprofile runs.

1) Evidence: no experiments have been run, so every design choice is uncertain. Priors from multimodal cellular profiling suggest that combining RNA and image modalities and aggregating multiple profiles per sample usually helps, but this is untested here. 2) Test: config_010 is a strong, representative multimodal multiprofile baseline. It uses scVI (n200) for RNA, ResNet50 for images, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. It tells us whether the full multimodal, multiprofile pipeline reaches high accuracy, and it serves as an anchor. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time: aggregation (avgpool), fusion (weighted), RNA encoder (scGPT or PCA), image encoder (ViT-L), or dropping to a single modality. 3) Why now: the likely winner sits in this region of the space, so a mid-cost representative is the most informative first step. It avoids the most expensive combinations (ViT-L image encoder plus scGPT RNA encoder) while still testing the key hypothesis. Expected relative cost: moderate-to-high. Multiprofile transformer aggregation with two modalities makes it costlier than single-profile or unimodal configs, but the compact scVI and ResNet50 encoders make it notably cheaper than the ViT-L or scGPT multimodal variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: we have one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile setup with scVI-200, ResNet50, transformer aggregation and concat fusion reached 0.579 accuracy (F1 0.563) for 5.16 GPU hours. With a single data point, we cannot yet tell which design axes drive performance. 2. What this tests: config_029 keeps every setting fixed except the image encoder, which changes from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Any accuracy change can therefore be attributed to the image backbone. The image representation is likely one of the highest-impact choices in the space, and ViT-L features are often stronger. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: if ViT-L helps, it points to the strongest branch of the search (ViT-L variants across RNA encoders and fusion types) for the remaining 8 experiments. If it does not help, we can stay with the cheaper ResNet50 and use the remaining runs on aggregation, fusion and RNA encoder. Expected relative cost: higher than config_010, roughly 1.5 to 2 times its 5.16 GPU hours, because of the larger ViT-L image representation. The large potential gain justifies that cost.

1) Evidence so far: with scVI RNA, transformer aggregation and concat fusion fixed, ResNet50 (0.579 acc / 0.563 F1) beat ViT-L (0.540 / 0.524). Both accuracy and F1 agree, so ResNet50 is the provisional image encoder, though this rests on one comparison. 2) This run keeps the best configuration (config_010) and swaps transformer aggregation for avgpool. That isolates whether the learned multiprofile aggregator is worth its cost, which is a major untested design choice. 3) It is the best next use of the budget for two reasons. It sits next to the current best, so it has a realistic chance of matching or beating it. Its result also decides the aggregation default for the remaining runs. If avgpool comes out comparable, later tests of RNA encoder and fusion can use the cheaper backbone. Expected cost: lower than config_010's 5.16 GPU hours because avgpool replaces the transformer, likely around 4 GPU hours.

1) Evidence: ResNet50 clearly beats ViT-L (0.579 vs 0.540 with the transformer and scVI held fixed). Avgpool is slightly ahead of the transformer (0.591 vs 0.579). That gap is small and comes from a single comparison, so it may not be reliable. Every run so far used scVI RNA embeddings and concat fusion, so the RNA encoder and fusion type are still completely unexplored. 2) This experiment keeps the current best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT. That isolates whether a foundation-model RNA representation improves accuracy. 3) The RNA encoder has two untested options and could plausibly shift accuracy more than the fusion choice. Testing it first on the best backbone is therefore the most informative next step, while still having a real chance of beating 0.591. The weighted-fusion test (config_003) can follow. Expected cost is similar to config_031, about 7 GPU hours, and possibly a bit more depending on scGPT's embedding size.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder has had the largest effect so far. Swapping scVI for scGPT, with resnet50, avgpool and concat held fixed, raised validation accuracy from 0.591 to 0.653 (F1 0.573 to 0.628). resnet50 beat imagenet_vit_l (0.579 vs 0.540), and avgpool slightly beat transformer (0.591 vs 0.579). These are single runs, so small gaps are uncertain. Fusion is the one design choice not yet tested: every run so far used concat. 2) Test: this experiment keeps the best configuration (scGPT, resnet50, multiprofile avgpool) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. That isolates the effect of fusion on the strongest base. 3) Why now: it exploits the clear scGPT gain while answering an open question that applies across the remaining search. Expected cost is similar to config_033 (about 4–5 GPU hours), since weighted fusion adds little compute and avgpool with resnet50 was the cheapest setup so far. If weighted fusion helps, later runs can build on it; if not, concat is confirmed and the budget can move to the pca_n2000 RNA encoder or single-profile alternatives.

1. Evidence: The RNA encoder is the most influential choice tested so far. Swapping scvi_n200 for scgpt in the resnet50/avgpool/concat setting raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.653, with F1 rising alongside it. Concat fusion clearly beats weighted fusion (0.653 vs 0.421). resnet50 has outperformed vit_l, and avgpool is slightly ahead of the transformer. The third RNA encoder, pca_n2000, has never been tested, so the most impactful dimension is still only partly explored. 2. Test: config_009 keeps the best-known setup (multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This is a clean single-variable comparison against config_033. It tells us whether scgpt is truly the best encoder or whether a high-dimensional PCA input can match or beat it. 3. Why now: Fusion and image encoder appear settled for the moment. Aggregation and modality ablations, such as scgpt with a transformer or RNA-only, are smaller refinements I can run with the remaining 3 experiments. Resolving the RNA encoder question now ensures later exploitation builds on the right encoder. Expected cost: moderate, about 4 to 7 GPU hours, similar to the other resnet50/avgpool multimodal runs. The 2000-dimensional PCA input may add slightly to cost, but it avoids the extra expense of a transformer or ViT.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. Switching it moved accuracy from 0.59 (scvi) to 0.65 (scgpt) to 0.715 (pca_n2000, config_009, the current best). Concat fusion clearly beats weighted (0.65 vs 0.42). ResNet50 beats ViT-L, and avgpool slightly beats transformer. The main untested question is whether the image branch helps at all, since no unimodal baseline has been run. 2) This experiment tests the PCA-2000 RNA-only multiprofile model with avgpool, which is config_009 without the image branch. If it matches or beats 0.715, imaging is adding little or even noise, and the last two runs should focus on RNA-only variants. If it falls clearly below, imaging contributes, and the remaining budget should go to PCA plus ResNet50 concat variants such as transformer aggregation or singleprofile. 3) It answers an important open design choice while staying close to the best region, so it has a real chance of becoming the new best. Expected cost: it drops image processing, so it should be well below config_009's 36 GPU hours. It is likely moderate, though the large 2000-dimensional PCA input may still make it costlier than the 4–7 hour scvi and scgpt runs.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is the RNA-only pca_n2000 avgpool multiprofile model (config_024: 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). It cost only 1.34 GPU hours. The multimodal pca_n2000 version with resnet50 (config_009) scored slightly lower at 0.715, despite costing 36.42 GPU hours. So the images do not appear to help, and pca_n2000 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder tested. Aggregation is the main design choice not yet tested in this setting. With scvi multimodal, transformer and avgpool were close (0.579 vs 0.591), which is a single, small comparison and not conclusive for the much stronger pca features. 2) Test: config_051 changes only the aggregation of the current best configuration, from avgpool to transformer. This shows whether attention-based multiprofile aggregation can extract more from the 2000-dimensional PCA features. 3) Why now: It directly exploits the leading direction while settling an open design choice. It is expected to be cheap, roughly 1.5–3 GPU hours, which is far below any multimodal pca run. That keeps total compute low and leaves two experiments for follow-up, such as single-profile RNA-only.

1. Evidence: The pca_n2000 RNA encoder is clearly the strongest. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (config_024) gives 0.725 accuracy for 1.34 GPU h. Adding ResNet50 images (config_009) did not help, scoring 0.715 for 36 GPU h. Transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool, and weighted fusion was clearly worse than concat. Image modality and alternative fusion choices therefore look unpromising. Profile setting is the one major design axis that remains completely untested: every run so far has been multiprofile. 2. Test: config_017 runs the best known encoder (pca_n2000, RNA-only) in the single-profile setting. This checks whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed, or whether a simpler single-profile model matches or beats 0.725. 3. Why this experiment: It is the most informative remaining test that still has a real chance of beating the current best. It is also very cheap, expected around 1 GPU h or less, since it has no aggregation and no image branch. That cost is far below the expensive multimodal alternatives such as pca with imagenet_vit_l, which the evidence suggests add little accuracy. It leaves budget for one final exploitation step.

1) Evidence: pca_n2000 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, reaching 0.715 to 0.725, versus at most 0.653 for scgpt and 0.591 for scvi. Concat fusion beats weighted fusion by a wide margin (0.653 vs 0.421). ResNet50 beats ViT-L (0.579 vs 0.540), and avgpool or no aggregation beats transformer aggregation. Single-profile RNA-only (0.721 at 0.04 GPU hours) nearly matches multiprofile RNA-only (0.725). Multiprofile multimodal pca+ResNet50+concat reached 0.715 but cost 36 GPU hours. 2) Test: config_032 combines the best components (pca_n2000, ResNet50, concat) in the cheaper single-profile setting. It checks whether adding image features without multiprofile aggregation can push past the 0.725 RNA-only best. 3) Why this choice for the last run: every other option includes a component already shown to be weaker (weighted fusion, transformer aggregation, ViT-L, or a non-pca encoder). This makes config_032 the best remaining chance at a new top score. Expected cost is low to moderate: far below the 36 GPU hours of multiprofile multimodal, likely a few GPU hours at most.

1) Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so the main uncertainty is whether combining RNA and image data (multimodal) and pooling several profiles per sample (multiprofile) actually help. Domain priors suggest both should beat RNA-only, image-only and single-profile setups. 2) Test: this run sets a central, mid-cost anchor in the region most likely to score well: multimodal, multiprofile, the compact scVI 200-dimensional RNA embedding, the ResNet50 image encoder, simple average pooling and concatenation fusion. Later runs can then change one factor at a time against it: switching to the transformer aggregator, to weighted fusion, to the larger ViT-L image encoder, to the scGPT or PCA-2000 RNA encoders, or dropping to a single modality. 3) Why now: starting at the most plausible region while avoiding the most expensive components (transformer aggregation, ViT-L, scGPT) gives a dependable baseline at moderate GPU cost. If the expensive upgrades help, the remaining 9 runs leave room to escalate to them. Expected relative cost: moderate. Multiprofile multimodal processing adds cost, but the low-dimensional scVI input, the lighter ResNet50 and average pooling keep it well below the ViT-L or transformer-based variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have only one result so far. config_013 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.530 accuracy and 0.515 F1 for 7.27 GPU hours. That gives a baseline but says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2. What this tests: config_033 is identical except that avgpool aggregation is replaced by transformer aggregation. Aggregation is the main way a multiprofile model combines its profiles, and learned attention over profiles could plausibly beat simple averaging. Because only one factor changes, any difference in accuracy can be attributed to it. 3. Why it is the best next use: Settling aggregation early tells us whether later experiments, such as trying ViT-L image features, scGPT RNA features or weighted fusion, should build on transformer or avgpool. That makes the remaining 8 experiments more efficient. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_013, perhaps around 8 to 10 GPU hours, because of the attention layers. That is still cheaper than switching to the larger ViT-L image encoder.

1. Evidence: with scvi_n200, resnet50 and concat fusion held fixed, transformer aggregation (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1) clearly beat avgpool (0.530 accuracy, 0.515 F1). Transformer was also cheaper (5.16 vs 7.27 GPU hours), so it is the anchor to keep. 2. Test: this run keeps the best configuration (config_033) and changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. That isolates whether a stronger pretrained image backbone adds accuracy on top of transformer aggregation. The image encoder is probably a larger lever than fusion type, which is a smaller tweak left for later. 3. Why now: we have 7 experiments left, and settling the image encoder early tells us which backbone to use for the later RNA-encoder (scgpt vs pca) and fusion comparisons. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_033, roughly 6 to 9 GPU hours, because ViT-L produces larger representations. That is justified because the image backbone could plausibly decide which configuration ends up best.

1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.650 vs 0.530 accuracy, with the same scvi_n200 + resnet50 + concat setup), and the F1 scores agree. ResNet50 slightly beat ViT-L under the transformer (0.650 vs 0.618), but that is a modest single comparison. The RNA encoder is the main untested axis: only scvi_n200 has been tried, and it has three options, so it could plausibly move accuracy more than fusion type. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (multiprofile, resnet50, transformer, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder to scGPT. It is a clean one-factor test of whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI. 3) It explores a high-impact axis while staying in the best-performing region, and the result will tell me whether to test PCA next or move on to weighted fusion (config_003, or its scGPT counterpart config_026). Expected cost is similar to config_033 (about 5 GPU hours), possibly slightly higher if scGPT embeddings are larger. That is still well below the 7.27-hour avgpool run.

1. Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.650 vs 0.530 with scvi_n200 + resnet50). ResNet50 slightly beats ViT-L (0.650 vs 0.619). scGPT and scVI are essentially tied (0.653 vs 0.650), but scGPT costs much more (9.06 vs 5.16 GPU hours). Fusion is the main design choice still untested: every run so far used concat. 2. Test: config_003 keeps the strong, cheap setup (multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer) and changes only fusion to weighted. Compared with config_033, this isolates the effect of fusion. 3. Why now: it reduces uncertainty on an important unexplored dimension with a single controlled change, on the cheaper of two near-equal RNA encoders. If weighted fusion helps, I can then try it with scGPT (config_026). Expected cost is moderate, about 5 GPU hours, similar to config_033 and roughly half of an scGPT run.

1) Evidence: three design choices look clear so far. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool by about 12 points (0.650 vs 0.530). Concat fusion beats weighted fusion by about 11 points (0.650 vs 0.535). ResNet50 edges out ViT-L (0.650 vs 0.619). Among RNA encoders, scGPT and scVI are nearly tied (0.653 vs 0.650, with similar F1), but scGPT cost about 75% more GPU time. The one major design choice still untested is the PCA_n2000 RNA encoder. 2) Test: config_010 places PCA_n2000 inside the best-performing setup (multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer, concat). This tells us whether a simpler, high-dimensional linear RNA representation matches or beats the learned encoders. 3) Why now: it fills the last important gap in the RNA-encoder dimension inside the strongest region of the search space. It therefore has a real chance of setting a new best, and it informs how the remaining 4 experiments are spent. Expected cost: moderate, likely similar to or slightly above the scVI transformer run (about 5–7 GPU hours) and below the scGPT run (about 9 GPU hours).

1. Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.650 vs 0.530). Concat fusion clearly beats weighted (0.650 vs 0.535). We do not know which part of this expensive setup drives the score. The most important and most cost-relevant unknown is whether multiprofile aggregation helps at all. 2. What this tests: config_004 changes only the profile setting to singleprofile. It keeps the same RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion, so the comparison isolates the value of multiprofile aggregation. 3. Why it is the best next step: the answer determines where the remaining 8 experiments go. If single-profile comes close to 0.619, later searches over encoders and fusion can use cheap single-profile runs. If it drops clearly, we can focus on multiprofile variants such as aggregation type and RNA encoder with confidence. Expected cost is substantially lower than config_043, roughly 30-50% of its 3.6 GPU hours, since no multiprofile aggregation is needed.

1) Evidence: with the scVI-n200 + ViT-L weighted-fusion backbone held fixed, the multiprofile transformer reached 0.619 accuracy (F1 0.610). The single-profile version reached 0.573. That is a solid gain of about 4.6 points, but it cost about 7x more (3.60 vs 0.53 GPU h). It is still unclear whether the gain comes from aggregating multiple profiles at all or from the transformer aggregator specifically. 2) Test: config_011 changes only the aggregation, from transformer to avgpool, so it isolates that choice. If avgpool matches or beats the transformer, the remaining budget can explore encoders and fusion on a cheaper multiprofile base. If it clearly loses, that supports keeping the transformer for the final exploitation steps. 3) Why now: aggregation is a high-impact choice that we have not yet tested, and the answer shapes both accuracy and cost for the other 6 experiments. Expected cost is moderate: still multiprofile and multimodal with ViT-L, but probably somewhat cheaper than the 3.6 GPU h transformer run, around 2.5-3 GPU h.

Evidence: across three runs, multiprofile with transformer aggregation (config_043, 0.619 acc / 0.610 F1) clearly beats singleprofile (0.573) and avgpool aggregation (0.422). So transformer-based multiprofile aggregation is the strongest direction so far. Uncertainty: the RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion type have each been tested at only one value (scvi_n200, ViT-L, weighted). Test: config_005 keeps the best setup and changes only the RNA encoder, from scvi_n200 to scGPT, as a clean one-factor comparison. Why now: the RNA representation is plausibly the largest remaining lever on accuracy. Exploiting the best architecture while varying one key factor balances exploitation with reducing uncertainty, leaving five later runs to probe fusion (e.g., config_047) or a cheaper ResNet50 encoder (config_010). Expected cost: similar to or slightly above config_043, about 3.5–4.5 GPU hours, since it is still multiprofile multimodal with transformer aggregation and scGPT embeddings may be somewhat larger.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_043 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.619 accuracy. Two design choices look settled. Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.619 vs 0.422 with everything else the same). scVI beats scGPT (0.619 vs 0.520). Multiprofile with transformer also beats singleprofile (0.573). Fusion has not been varied at all, since every run so far used weighted fusion. 2) Test: config_047 changes only the fusion, from weighted to concat, on the best configuration. This cleanly tells us whether concat fusion helps the leading setup. 3) Why now: It exploits the strongest direction while closing the largest untested design gap. Changing just one factor makes the result easy to interpret. The answer tells us which fusion to use in later tests of PCA RNA features and the ResNet50 image encoder. Expected cost is similar to config_043, about 3.5–4 GPU hours, since it uses the same multiprofile transformer and ViT-L setup. That is moderately expensive, but justified because it is the most likely candidate to improve on the current best.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_043 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion), at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Changing a single component from that setup gave clear drops. Transformer beat avgpool (0.62 vs 0.42), weighted fusion beat concat (0.62 vs 0.21), and scVI beat scGPT (0.62 vs 0.52). Since the RNA encoder has shown the largest single-swap effect apart from fusion and aggregation, which are now settled, this is the most likely route to a new best within the remaining budget. Swapping the image encoder to ResNet50 can follow later as a cheaper check. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.619 accuracy / 0.610 F1. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Changing any single component from it made results worse. scGPT and PCA encoders gave about 0.52, ResNet50 gave 0.53, avgpool gave 0.42, concat fusion gave 0.21, and single-profile gave 0.57. Test: config_027 keeps the strongest components (scVI n200 encoder and transformer multiprofile aggregation) but removes the image modality. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is the cheap RNA-only scVI multiprofile transformer (config_027, 0.629 acc, 0.40 GPU h). The best multimodal run (config_043, 0.619) scored slightly lower on accuracy, slightly higher on F1 (0.610 vs 0.599), and cost 9x more. So adding images has not clearly helped. Two design choices look settled: transformer aggregation beat avgpool by a wide margin, and weighted fusion beat concat by a wide margin. The RNA encoder is the main open lever. In multimodal runs scVI beat PCA (0.523) and scGPT (0.520), but those comparisons are confounded by the image branch and fusion. 2) Test: config_022 swaps scVI for PCA-2000 inside the winning RNA-only multiprofile transformer setup. PCA was marginally ahead of scGPT in the multimodal comparison and avoids foundation-model embedding overhead. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200 with a transformer (config_027, 0.629 acc), slightly ahead of its multimodal weighted counterpart (0.619). The image branch seems to add little. Several factors look clearly harmful: avgpool cost about 0.20 accuracy, scgpt about 0.10, pca about 0.10 to 0.20, and concat fusion was catastrophic. The mildest penalty seen was singleprofile versus multiprofile in the multimodal setting, about 0.046. 2) This experiment tests whether the strongest RNA-only setup (scvi_n200) works as well or better without multiprofile aggregation. Without the image branch and aggregation noise, a simpler model could match or exceed config_027. 3) Since this is the final experiment, the other candidates near the best are weak bets. scgpt RNA-only, scvi avgpool and image-only all have direct evidence of larger drops. Among them, this option has the smallest expected gap to the current best, so it has the best chance of setting a new best. It should also be the cheapest option, likely under 0.4 GPU hours, comparable to or below config_027.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence on any axis: modality, profile setting, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. Priors from multimodal profiling suggest that combining RNA and image modalities, and aggregating over multiple profiles, both tend to improve accuracy. 2) config_004 tests that prior with a mid-range setup: multimodal, multiprofile, the compact scvi_n200 RNA encoder, the strong imagenet_vit_l image encoder, cheap avgpool aggregation and simple concat fusion. It avoids the costliest components (scgpt, transformer aggregation) while keeping the likely highest-value ones. 3) It is a strong anchor result early in the budget. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time: transformer vs. avgpool aggregation, scgpt or PCA vs. scVI, weighted vs. concat fusion, or unimodal and single-profile ablations.
