Evidence: the best result so far is config_041 (pca_n2000 + resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. The same setup with weighted fusion reached 0.678, and transformer aggregation was consistently worse. The PCA RNA encoder appears to drive the strong results: with resnet50, PCA scored 0.72 while scVI scored 0.41 and scGPT 0.52. Image results are mixed, since PCA with ViT-L scored only 0.47, so it is unclear how much the image branch contributes. Test: config_026 keeps the strongest elements (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and drops the image branch. It is the one untested setup that could plausibly match or beat 0.72, since noisy image features may be adding little or even hurting. Alternatives are weaker bets: further fusion and transformer variants have underperformed, and scGPT and scVI pairings with resnet50 were clearly worse. Why now: as the last experiment, it gives a real chance at a new best and also settles the important question of whether multimodality is needed. Expected cost is low, likely under 5 GPU hours and well below config_041's 36 GPU hours, because it skips image processing.

1. Evidence: No experiments have been run yet. Prior expectations from multimodal cell-profiling work are that combining RNA and image modalities, and aggregating over multiple profiles, are the design choices most likely to drive accuracy. Which encoders and fusion method matter most is still uncertain. 2. What this tests: config_030 is a strong but moderately priced anchor in the likely-best region: multimodal, multiprofile, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. It uses the compact scVI-200 RNA encoder and the cheaper ResNet50 image encoder. The result gives a high baseline that later runs can compare against. Those runs can swap in ViT-L, scGPT or PCA, weighted fusion, or avgpool, or drop a modality, to isolate the effect of each choice. 3. Why now: It goes after high accuracy early while avoiding the most expensive combination (ViT-L plus scGPT plus transformer). 1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. The full multimodal, multiprofile model (scVI RNA, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1 at 5.16 GPU hours. With a single data point, the impact of each design choice is still unknown. The image encoder is one of the most consequential choices: a large pretrained ViT-L often gives much richer morphology features than ResNet50. 2. What this tests: config_002 changes only the image encoder (ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L) and keeps everything else fixed. This gives a clean comparison that tells us whether image representation quality is a major lever. 3. Why this is the best next use: if ViT-L helps substantially, the rest of the search can be anchored on it. If it does not, later runs can use the cheaper ResNet50 and focus on the RNA encoder, aggregation or fusion. Expected cost is higher than the 5.16 GPU hour baseline, roughly 1.3 to 2 times, because of the larger encoder within a multiprofile multimodal setup. I judge this worthwhile because the image encoder is a likely source of the best accuracy.

1) Evidence so far: only two runs, both multimodal, multiprofile, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. Swapping the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l improved accuracy (0.485 to 0.512) and F1 (0.464 to 0.477) at slightly lower cost (4.65 vs 5.16 GPU h). That makes vit_l the current best image encoder. The RNA encoder is still untested, and it is one of the most important remaining design choices. 2) This run keeps the best setup fixed (multiprofile, vit_l, transformer, concat) and swaps scvi_n200 for scgpt. Because only one factor changes, the result directly shows whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI. 3) This is the best use of the next run because it explores a high-impact axis while staying in the strongest region found so far. The outcome tells us which RNA encoder to carry into later tests of fusion (weighted) and aggregation (avgpool). Expected cost is about the same as config_002, roughly 4.5–5.5 GPU hours, possibly a little higher if the scGPT embeddings are larger.

1) Evidence: switching the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scGPT, with the ViT-L image encoder, transformer aggregation and concat fusion all held fixed, raised validation accuracy from 0.512 to 0.619. F1 rose similarly, from 0.477 to 0.610. ViT-L also beat ResNet50 under scVI (0.512 vs 0.485). Fusion strategy has never been varied, so it is the main untested design choice around the current best setup. 2) Test: config_036 keeps the best configuration (config_017) and changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted. This isolates whether weighted fusion helps on top of the strong scGPT + ViT-L + transformer combination. 3) Why now: it is a focused exploitation step that also resolves an open design question, and the result directly guides later choices, such as whether to then test avgpool aggregation with the better fusion. Expected cost is similar to config_017, roughly 4 GPU hours, because the architecture and encoders are unchanged. That makes it a moderate-cost experiment with a high chance of matching or beating the current best.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_017 (scGPT + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Two patterns stand out. Swapping scVI for scGPT gave a large gain of about 0.10. Weighted fusion was clearly worse than concat (0.530 vs 0.619). Every run so far has used transformer aggregation, so the aggregation choice is completely untested. 2) Test: config_023 keeps the best encoders and concat fusion but uses avgpool aggregation. This isolates whether a simpler aggregation matches or beats the transformer in the strongest setting. 3) Why now: It is a one-factor change from the current best, so it exploits that configuration while settling an important open design choice. The result will guide the remaining 5 experiments, for example whether to try PCA or ResNet variants under the better aggregation. Expected cost: lower than the transformer runs, probably about 2.5–3.5 GPU hours, because avgpool is lighter than transformer aggregation.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_017 (scGPT + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Changing one factor at a time from that setup lowered accuracy each time. Swapping to weighted fusion gave 0.530, avgpool aggregation gave 0.224, and the scVI encoder gave 0.512 with ViT-L. So transformer aggregation and concat fusion look clearly preferable. The RNA encoder had the largest effect among the encoders, with scGPT about 0.10 above scVI. The remaining open question is the third encoder, pca_n2000, which has never been tested. 2. Test: config_011 keeps the best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This tells us whether a simple high-dimensional PCA representation can match or beat scGPT, finishing the encoder comparison inside the best-performing setup. 3. Why now: Encoder choice has shown the biggest effect, so this is the most likely remaining single change to beat 0.619. The other main options mostly target secondary questions: unimodal or single-profile variants are probably cheaper but less likely to win, and further fusion or aggregation changes have already been shown to hurt. Expected cost is moderate, similar to config_017 and config_002 at about 4-5 GPU hours, since it uses the same transformer and ViT-L multiprofile pipeline. The 2000-dimensional PCA input may add slightly more cost than scGPT.

Evidence: config_017 (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) is the best so far at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Ablations around it point consistently in one direction. Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.224). Concat beats weighted fusion (0.530). scGPT beats PCA (0.573) and scVI (0.512). ViT-L beats ResNet50 under scVI (0.512 vs 0.485). Uncertainty: the profile setting is a major design choice that has never been tested, since all six runs were multiprofile. Test: config_013 keeps the strongest components (scGPT, ViT-L, concat) but switches to single-profile input. This shows whether multiprofile aggregation is really needed or whether the strong encoder pair alone carries performance. Why now: with 3 experiments left, this settles the last untested core axis, and the result decides how to spend the remaining runs (multiprofile variants such as scGPT + ResNet50 or an RNA-only transformer, versus single-profile variants). Expected cost: low. With no multiprofile aggregation, it should be cheaper than the roughly 4 GPU hours of config_017, likely about 1–3 GPU hours.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_017 (scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer, concat) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Several design choices look settled. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool by a wide margin (0.62 vs 0.22). Concat fusion beats weighted fusion (0.62 vs 0.53). scGPT is the strongest RNA encoder (scGPT 0.62 > PCA 0.57 > scVI 0.51). Multiprofile beats singleprofile (0.62 vs 0.54). ViT-L beat ResNet50 with scVI (0.51 vs 0.48). The key untested question is whether the image branch helps at all. Concat fusion clearly outperformed weighted fusion, which hints that RNA carries most of the signal. 2) This experiment: an RNA-only scGPT model with multiprofile transformer aggregation. It directly tests whether the strongest RNA pathway alone can match or beat the multimodal best. If it does, it becomes the new best; if not, it confirms the image branch is useful and lets the last two runs refine around config_017. 3) Why now: Swapping ViT-L for ResNet50 (config_007) is likely to score lower given the earlier ResNet50 result. The RNA-only ablation is the most informative remaining question about an important design choice, and it has realistic upside. Expected cost is relatively low, roughly 2–3 GPU hours, below the 4–5 hours of multimodal multiprofile runs, because there is no image encoder processing.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_017 (scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer, concat) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Three of its design choices are each supported by a single test. Changing the RNA encoder to PCA dropped accuracy to 0.573, and scVI dropped it to 0.512. Changing fusion to weighted dropped it to 0.530. Changing aggregation to avgpool dropped it to 0.224. Moving to single-profile dropped it to 0.540. The image encoder is the one axis not yet tested on the scGPT backbone. With scVI, ResNet50 was only about 0.03 below ViT-L (0.485 vs 0.512), a small gap that may depend on the RNA encoder. 2) Test: config_007 changes only the image encoder in the best configuration. It shows whether ResNet50 matches or beats ViT-L when paired with scGPT. That would settle the last open choice in the leading configuration. 3) Rationale: Every other untested neighbour of the best configuration uses weighted fusion, avgpool, single-profile or a weaker RNA encoder, all of which hurt. Image-only runs seem unlikely to beat 0.619, since swapping the RNA encoder moved accuracy by about 0.1. This one-factor variant is therefore the most plausible way to raise the best score. It also leaves the final experiment free for exploitation. Expected cost is moderate, about 4–5 GPU hours, similar to other multiprofile transformer runs (roughly 4–5 GPU hours each).

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_017 (scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. The other tested choices all did worse than the matching config_017 setting: avgpool aggregation (0.22), weighted fusion (0.53), ResNet50 (0.54), single-profile (0.54) and the scVI or PCA encoders (0.51 and 0.57). Every multiprofile transformer concat run with ViT-L has now been tested. The remaining untested combinations each change one of these settings in a way that has already hurt accuracy. Why now: on the final run, the other options are weighted-fusion, ResNet50, avgpool or single-profile variants, and all of these are predicted to fall below 0.619. Test: config_019 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, with everything else held fixed. 1) Evidence: Three experiments point the same way. The scVI-200 + ResNet50 + transformer + concat configuration (config_017) reached 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_017 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + concat, 0.725 acc). Three single changes from it all hurt. Swapping the image encoder to ViT-L dropped accuracy to 0.33. Swapping the RNA encoder to scGPT dropped it to 0.47. Switching fusion to weighted dropped it to 0.64. Concat fusion and ResNet50 look settled, and the RNA encoder is clearly a high-impact choice. The third RNA option, pca_n2000, has never been tested. 2) Test: config_012 keeps every component of the best config and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. 1) Evidence: config_017 (scVI n200 + ResNet50 + transformer + concat) leads at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. One-factor changes from it all did worse. Swapping to the ViT-L image encoder dropped accuracy to 0.33. Swapping the RNA encoder to scGPT or PCA gave 0.47–0.51. Swapping concat for weighted fusion gave 0.64. These are single runs, but the gaps are large, so scVI, ResNet50 and concat look like the right choices. Aggregation is still untested: every run so far used the transformer. 2) This run keeps the best setup and changes only transformer to avgpool. It shows whether the transformer aggregator is what drives performance, or whether simpler pooling matches or beats it. 3) Aggregation is the main design choice left open around the current best, so this run is the most informative next step. It can either beat 0.725 directly or confirm that the transformer should be kept for the remaining runs. Expected cost is somewhat lower than config_017's 5.16 GPU hours, probably around 4–5, since avgpool is lighter than a transformer and ResNet50 with scVI are the cheaper encoders.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_017 (scVI + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. Swapping in avgpool aggregation gave 0.713 with slightly higher F1, so aggregation matters little. Weighted fusion hurt (0.639). scVI clearly beats scGPT and PCA. ViT-L images collapsed accuracy to 0.33, so the image branch has a large effect, but we cannot yet tell whether ResNet50 images add signal or are only less harmful than ViT-L. 2) Test: config_005 is the RNA-only counterpart of config_017, using the same scVI encoder and transformer aggregation with no image branch. It measures how much the image modality adds. If it matches or beats 0.725, the remaining two runs should go to RNA-only variants. If it falls well short, multimodal with ResNet50 is confirmed and the final runs can refine around config_017. 3) Why now: modality choice is the largest remaining design question that has not been tested. Answering it directs the last two experiments, and it has a real chance of setting a new best given the strong scVI signal. Expected cost is lower than the multimodal runs, likely about 3–4 GPU hours versus 5–7, since there is no image encoder or fusion step.

1) Evidence: the scVI RNA encoder drives performance. Multimodal scVI+ResNet50 with transformer reached 0.725 accuracy (config_017), and RNA-only scVI with transformer nearly matched it at 0.721 (config_005) for only 0.40 GPU hours. So the image branch adds little at roughly 13x the cost. In the multimodal setting, avgpool aggregation gave slightly lower accuracy (0.713) but the best F1 (0.695), so the choice of aggregation is still unresolved. 2) This run tests avgpool aggregation in the cheap RNA-only scVI multiprofile setting, to see whether it can match or beat the current best accuracy. 3) It is the best use of the remaining budget because it is expected to be very cheap (about 0.4 GPU hours, far below the 5-9 hours of multimodal runs) and probes a plausible route to a new best. Its result will also show whether the last experiment should refine the RNA-only line or go back to multimodal variants.

1) Evidence: scVI-n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (scGPT and PCA scored about 0.47 to 0.51), ResNet50 is far better than ViT-L (0.33), and concat beats weighted fusion with a transformer (0.725 vs 0.639). The best result, config_017 at 0.725, is barely above the RNA-only scVI transformer (0.721) at a fraction of the cost, so images add little in the multiprofile setting. Every completed run used multiprofile, so the profile setting is the largest untested design axis. 2) This run keeps the best components (scVI, ResNet50, concat) and switches to singleprofile, with no aggregation module. It tests whether per-profile modeling can match or beat multiprofile aggregation. It also shows whether the images contribute more when cells are not pooled. 3) Under-explored scVI+ResNet multiprofile variants remain, but they mostly recombine choices already shown to be weaker (avgpool, weighted fusion). This run is the most informative remaining test with a realistic chance of a new best. The caveat is that RNA results dropped sharply with avgpool, which hints that set-level modeling matters, so a drop here is plausible. Even a weaker result is useful: it would confirm multiprofile and point the final experiment back toward refining config_017. Expected cost is moderate, likely lower than the 5 to 7 GPU-hour multiprofile multimodal runs, since there is no multiprofile aggregation.

1. Evidence: scVI-n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (scGPT reached 0.47 and PCA 0.51). ResNet50 is far better than ViT-L (ViT-L reached 0.33). Within the scVI+ResNet50 multiprofile family, transformer+concat is best (0.725), avgpool+concat is close (0.713, with the highest F1 of 0.695), and transformer+weighted is lower (0.639). 2. Question: config_027 (scVI+ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) is the only untested cell in this top-performing family. It tests whether weighted fusion behaves differently under avgpool aggregation, where the setup already shows strong F1. 3. Why this one: on the final experiment, only a configuration near the current best has a realistic chance of beating 0.725. Options built on scGPT, PCA, ViT-L or singleprofile all have strong evidence of lower accuracy. Image-only and RNA-only alternatives also look unlikely to beat it, because RNA-only scVI already roughly matches the multimodal result. The chance of improving is modest, since weighted fusion underperformed with the transformer, but this is still the most plausible candidate left. Expected cost is relatively high, about 6–7.5 GPU hours, similar to config_047 and config_003.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet. The two biggest open design choices are multimodal vs. single-modality and multiprofile aggregation vs. single profiles. Domain priors suggest that combining RNA and image data, and aggregating several profiles, should raise accuracy, but this is unconfirmed. 2. What this tests: config_034 sets a mid-cost anchor for the multimodal + multiprofile family. If it scores well, later runs can test each upgrade in turn: a transformer aggregator, a ViT-L image encoder, scGPT embeddings, or weighted fusion. Why now: it sits in the likely-best region of the search space without paying for the most expensive components on the first try. 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_034 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.523 accuracy and 0.508 F1. That is one data point, so every design choice is still uncertain. 2. Test: config_020 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer. This gives a clean one-variable comparison against the baseline. Why now: aggregation is a key design choice in multiprofile models, and a transformer is a plausible source of accuracy gains. 1) Evidence so far: both runs use multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50 and concat fusion. Avgpool (0.523 acc, 0.508 F1) slightly beat transformer aggregation (0.512 acc, 0.477 F1). The higher F1 supports avgpool as the better default, but the gap is small. Image encoder, RNA encoder and fusion are all still untested. 2) This run keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. That cleanly isolates what is likely one of the most influential choices, since stronger visual representations often drive multimodal profiling performance. 3) It exploits the current best setting while resolving a major uncertainty early, so the remaining 7 runs can target RNA encoder and fusion on the stronger image backbone. Expected cost is relatively high, because it is multimodal, multiprofile and uses ViT-L features. It should still be cheaper than the transformer-aggregation version, which is a reasonable trade-off for a strong first anchor.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: we have only one result. The multimodal, multiprofile config (scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) reached 0.530 accuracy and 0.515 F1. That gives a baseline but says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2) What this tests: config_019 is identical except that avgpool is replaced by transformer aggregation. This one-variable change isolates whether learned attention across a cell's multiple profiles beats simple mean pooling. Aggregation is likely one of the highest-impact choices for multiprofile models, and the answer applies to many of the remaining configs. 3) Why it is the best next use of the budget: it exploits the only known working setup while settling a key design question. If it helps, later experiments can vary the RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion under transformer aggregation. If it does not, we stay with the cheaper avgpool and explore elsewhere. Expected cost is moderately higher than the 2.94 GPU-hour baseline, roughly 1.2–1.5x, because of the extra transformer aggregator. That is justified because it is a plausible candidate for the best accuracy.

1. Evidence: the two completed runs (scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile, weighted fusion) differ only in aggregation and score almost the same (0.5305 vs 0.5318 accuracy, with similar F1). Aggregation is therefore not a strong lever here, while the RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion choices are still untested. 2. Test: this run keeps the slightly better transformer/weighted/ViT-L setup and swaps the scGPT RNA encoder for scVI (n200). It isolates whether the RNA representation, a likely high-impact factor, can lift accuracy above about 0.53. 3. Why now: changing a single important factor against the current best gives a clean comparison and reduces the biggest remaining uncertainty early in the budget. If scVI helps, later runs can explore fusion and image-encoder variants around it. Expected cost is about the same as previous runs, roughly 2.9 GPU hours for multimodal multiprofile with ViT-L. The scVI encoder is lighter than scGPT, so it may be marginally cheaper.

1) Evidence: All three completed runs used multiprofile, multimodal, ImageNet ViT-L and weighted fusion. Accuracies sit within about 0.005 (0.527 to 0.532), so aggregation (transformer vs. avgpool) and RNA encoder (scGPT vs. scVI) look like minor factors. scGPT with transformer aggregation (config_019) is currently best at 0.532, but the margin is too small to call decisive. Fusion type has never been varied, which leaves it as the largest open design question. 2) Test: config_030 changes only fusion, from weighted to concat, on the current best setup. This cleanly isolates the effect of fusion. 3) Why now: A single-variable change from the best configuration both exploits that configuration and resolves a major unexplored axis. The result will tell us whether later runs should use concat or weighted fusion, before spending budget on other axes such as image encoder or PCA RNA. Expected cost is similar to config_019, about 2.9 GPU hours, since the architecture is otherwise identical and concat fusion is no more expensive than weighted.

1. Evidence: All four tests used the imagenet_vit_l image encoder with multiprofile multimodal inputs. Weighted fusion beat concat (0.532 vs 0.518, and a much larger F1 gap). Transformer and avgpool aggregation were nearly tied (0.532 vs 0.530). scGPT edged out scVI (0.532 vs 0.527). The image encoder is a major design choice that is still completely untested. 2. Test: config_034 keeps the best setup (config_019: scGPT, transformer, weighted, multiprofile) and changes only the image encoder to resnet50. This gives a clean single-factor answer on whether ViT-L is needed or a CNN works as well or better. 3. Why now: Changing aggregation or RNA encoder again would likely yield only small gains. The image encoder question could shift the whole remaining search, either toward cheaper resnet50 configurations or by confirming ViT-L for exploitation. Expected cost is moderate, likely somewhat below the ViT-L runs at roughly 2-2.5 GPU hours, because resnet50 features are smaller.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The image encoder is by far the strongest factor so far. Switching from ViT-L to ResNet50 raised validation accuracy from about 0.53 to 0.706, and F1 rose from 0.516 to 0.667. Under ViT-L, the aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) made almost no difference, and weighted fusion beat concat. The RNA encoder was only compared between scGPT and scVI, which were close. PCA_n2000 has never been tested, so whether a different RNA representation adds value on top of the stronger ResNet50 features is an open question. 2. What this tests: config_021 keeps everything from the best configuration (multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder to PCA_n2000. That isolates an untested RNA representation within the winning setup. 3. Why it is the best next step: it exploits the ResNet50 result while reducing uncertainty about the one design axis still unexplored, and it either finds a better configuration or confirms scGPT for the remaining 4 experiments. Expected cost is high, similar to config_034 at roughly 10–12 GPU hours. That is justified because ResNet50 multimodal is the only region likely to produce the best accuracy, and PCA features are not expected to add cost over scGPT.

1) Evidence: The only strong result is config_034 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + weighted) at 0.706 accuracy. Every ImageNet ViT-L variant plateaued at about 0.52-0.53. ResNet50 does not help on its own: with PCA RNA (config_021) it reached only 0.52. So the gain seems to come from scGPT combined with ResNet50. Among the ViT runs, weighted fusion beat concat, scGPT slightly beat scVI, and avgpool vs transformer aggregation made almost no difference (0.530 vs 0.532). 2) Test: config_047 keeps the winning scGPT + ResNet50 + weighted combination and swaps transformer aggregation for avgpool. This isolates whether aggregation matters in the high-performing regime. Transformer aggregation did not matter for ViT, so avgpool has a real chance of matching or beating 0.706. 3) Why now: it exploits the strongest direction while answering a remaining design question. Avgpool should cost less than transformer aggregation, so I expect it to be somewhat cheaper than config_034's 12.31 GPU hours, while still multiprofile and multimodal and far above the ViT runs. That leaves budget for testing scVI with ResNet50 (config_037) or other refinements later.

1) Evidence: ResNet50 with transformer aggregation and weighted fusion is the clear winner so far. config_034 (scGPT) reached 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1, well above every ViT-L run (about 0.52-0.53). The RNA encoder matters strongly in the ResNet50 setting: PCA dropped the same architecture to 0.520 (config_021). The ViT runs suggest scVI is close to scGPT (0.527 vs 0.532). Concat fusion hurt with ViT, and avgpool fell below transformer with ResNet50 (0.586 vs 0.706). 2) Test: this swaps only the RNA encoder to scVI in the best architecture. It checks whether scVI can match or beat scGPT where the encoder choice clearly matters, which is the most plausible remaining route past 0.706. 3) Why now: it is a one-change extension of the best result, unlike concat (already shown worse) or riskier image-only runs. Expected cost is high, similar to or somewhat below config_034's 12.3 GPU hours, judging by scVI ViT runs that were only slightly more expensive than scGPT. That cost is justified because this configuration is the most likely new best.

1. Evidence: config_034 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + weighted) is clearly best at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Swapping out any one of its components hurt badly: avgpool gave 0.586, and replacing scGPT with PCA or scVI gave 0.520 and 0.422. Fusion type is the only design choice not yet tested on this strong backbone. The single concat-vs-weighted comparison (ViT-L, 0.518 vs 0.532) is small, comes from a much weaker setting and may not transfer, given the strong encoder interactions seen with ResNet50. 2. This experiment tests whether concat fusion can match or beat weighted fusion on the best-known backbone, with everything else held fixed. 3. Why it is the best use of the slot: it is the most direct remaining neighbor of the leader and the most plausible way to exceed 0.706. Single-profile, image-only and RNA-only variants all remove parts the evidence suggests are essential (transformer aggregation over profiles, and the scGPT-ResNet50 pairing). Expected cost is high, about 12-14 GPU hours (similar to or slightly above config_034, since concat ran costlier than weighted with ViT-L). That cost is justified because this region is where the best accuracy is found.

Evidence: scGPT + ResNet50 is by far the strongest pairing. The best result is config_049 (transformer, concat) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1, followed by config_034 (transformer, weighted) at 0.706. With ResNet50, swapping scGPT for PCA or scVI dropped accuracy to 0.42-0.52, so the other RNA encoders are not worth trying. Within scGPT + ResNet50, avgpool with weighted fusion (config_047) reached 0.586. Question: the one untested cell of the aggregation x fusion grid in this family is avgpool with concat. Concat beat weighted under transformer aggregation, especially on F1. This run tests whether concat also lifts the avgpool variant and whether that variant can match the transformer result. Why this run: with one experiment left, an untested near neighbour of the best family has a better chance of approaching the 0.713 best than more distant options. Those include image-only, single-profile, or scVI/PCA configurations, which existing evidence suggests are weaker. I don't expect this run to clearly beat 0.713, because avgpool lagged transformer by about 0.12 under weighted fusion. Expected cost is moderate, about 4-6 GPU hours, cheaper than the 9-12 hour transformer ResNet50 runs.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so I am relying on priors. Combining RNA and imaging, and aggregating over multiple profiles, usually beats a single modality or a single profile. Which encoder, aggregation and fusion choices work best is still unknown. 2) What this tests: it sets a strong first anchor. It is multimodal and multiprofile, uses the compact scVI (200-dim) RNA latent, the ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, transformer aggregation and simple concat fusion. Later runs can ablate one factor at a time from this point: avgpool vs transformer, scGPT or PCA vs scVI, ResNet50 vs ViT-L, weighted vs concat, and unimodal baselines. 3) Why now: with 10 runs, starting near the likely high-accuracy region gives a competitive result early, so later runs can either exploit it or show whether cheaper variants match it. Expected relative cost is high, roughly among the most expensive options, because it combines multiprofile transformer aggregation with ViT-L features. The low-dimensional scVI input keeps it somewhat cheaper than the PCA-2000 or scGPT versions.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. config_011 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, transformer, concat) reached 0.512 accuracy and 0.477 F1 at 4.65 GPU hours. We do not yet know whether the expensive ViT-L image branch adds any accuracy. 2. What this tests: config_036 removes the image branch and keeps everything else the same (scVI encoder, multiprofile, transformer aggregation). This directly measures how much the image modality contributes. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.512, the remaining budget can go to cheaper RNA-centric variants such as other RNA encoders and aggregation choices. If it falls clearly short, image information matters and later experiments should focus on multimodal settings, such as fusion type and image encoder. 3. Why it is the best next step: modality is the highest-level design choice, and a clean one-factor ablation of it reduces the most uncertainty per experiment. Dropping the ViT-L branch should make this run substantially cheaper than config_011, likely well under half its cost.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile transformer with scVI (config_036) reached 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1 for only 0.40 GPU h. Multimodal concat with ViT-L (config_011) did much worse, at 0.512 accuracy for 4.65 GPU h. That suggests the image branch or concat fusion adds noise, though one run is not conclusive. The biggest open question in the strong, cheap RNA-only line is the RNA encoder. config_009 keeps the winning multiprofile transformer setup and swaps scVI for scGPT. This isolates whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI. The result will also tell us which RNA encoder to carry into later multimodal runs, for example with weighted fusion. Expected cost is low: likely about 0.4 to 0.8 GPU h, slightly above config_036 because scGPT embeddings are larger, and far below any multimodal ViT-L run. This makes it an efficient experiment that can both improve the best score and reduce uncertainty.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with a multiprofile transformer (0.619 acc, 0.610 F1), and it was cheap at 0.40 GPU h. Swapping in scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.328, so the choice of RNA encoder matters a lot. Adding ImageNet ViT-L images with concat fusion lowered accuracy to 0.512 and cost 4.65 GPU h. The third RNA encoder, pca_n2000, is still untested, which is the largest open question about a design choice that clearly drives performance. 2. Test: config_040 keeps the winning setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) and only swaps the encoder to PCA-2000. This isolates whether PCA can beat scVI. The answer also tells us which RNA encoder to carry into any later multimodal or aggregation experiments. 3. Why now: Expected cost is low, about 0.4–0.6 GPU h, similar to the earlier RNA-only runs and far below multimodal ViT-L runs. It could plausibly produce a new best, and it narrows the search cheaply before more expensive multimodal configurations are tried.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder matters most so far. pca_n2000 (0.713 acc, 0.695 F1) clearly beats scvi_n200 (0.619) and scgpt (0.328) under the same rna_only, multiprofile, transformer setup. The one multimodal run (scvi + ViT-L, concat) scored 0.512, well below scvi rna_only at 0.619. That suggests naive concatenation of image features may hurt, but it is a single run and fusion type has not been tested. 2) This experiment pairs the best RNA encoder (pca_n2000) with resnet50 under transformer aggregation and weighted fusion. It tests whether weighted fusion can down-weight noisy image features so that image information adds to the strong PCA baseline rather than degrading it. 3) Why now: Whether multimodal fusion can beat rna_only is the largest remaining question, and it determines whether to spend the remaining budget on multimodal or rna_only variants. Using resnet50 instead of ViT-L gives an informative multimodal test at moderate cost. I expect it to cost roughly 2-3 GPU hours: more than the ~1 h rna_only runs but well under the 4.65 h ViT-L run. If it fails, cheap rna_only follow-ups remain, such as config_015 (PCA with avgpool) and config_016 (PCA single-profile).

Evidence: RNA-only models clearly lead. The best is pca_n2000 with multiprofile transformer aggregation (0.713 acc, 0.695 F1), ahead of scvi_n200 (0.619) and scgpt (0.328). Both multimodal runs scored lower (0.48-0.51) and cost far more (4.6-6.6 GPU h each), so adding images has not helped so far. The main open question is aggregation, because every run used a transformer. This experiment keeps the best encoder and profile setting (pca_n2000, multiprofile, RNA-only) and swaps the transformer for avgpool. That tells us whether simpler pooling matches or beats the transformer, which matters for all remaining choices. With 4 experiments left, it is a low-risk way to improve on or confirm the current best. Expected cost is low, about 0.5-1 GPU h, likely below config_040's 0.99 GPU h and far below any multimodal run.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only pca_n2000 with multiprofile transformer aggregation (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). PCA clearly beats scVI (0.619) and scGPT (0.328) as the RNA encoder. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool for PCA (0.713 vs 0.678). Both multimodal runs were much worse than their RNA-only counterparts (0.51 and 0.48) and cost the most (4.7 to 6.6 GPU hours), so adding image features currently looks harmful. 2) Open question: the profile setting has not been tested at all, since every run so far was multiprofile. This experiment keeps the best RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and switches to singleprofile. It shows whether multiprofile aggregation actually adds value or whether a simpler per-profile model is as good or better. 3) Why now: this is the main untested design axis within the strongest branch of the search. It is also likely the cheapest option, well under 1 GPU hour, because it has no aggregation module and no image branch. The answer will tell me whether to spend the last two experiments on refining multiprofile RNA-only or on singleprofile variants. Expected cost: low, roughly 0.3 to 0.8 GPU hours.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_040 (RNA-only, pca_n2000, transformer, 0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). For RNA encoders, pca_n2000 beats scvi_n200 (0.619), which beats scgpt (0.328). Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.678), and multiprofile beats singleprofile (0.519). The untested RNA-only options use weaker encoders or single profiles, so none of them is likely to beat 0.713. The only realistic route to a higher score is adding images to the winning RNA setup. The two multimodal runs so far both scored poorly, but each confounds several factors. config_008 paired pca_n2000 with resnet50 and weighted fusion. config_011 paired the weaker scvi_n200 encoder with ViT-L and concat. The combination of the best RNA encoder, ViT-L and concat fusion has not been tested. 2) Test: config_005 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) checks whether the stronger image encoder and simpler fusion can add useful information to the best RNA pipeline. If it does not, that confirms RNA-only is the ceiling. 3) Why now: this is the only remaining direction with a plausible chance of exceeding 0.713, and it leaves one experiment to follow up (for example, weighted fusion in config_034) or stop. Expected cost is high, about 5–7 GPU hours, similar to config_011 and config_008 and well above the 1 GPU hour of the RNA-only runs. That cost is justified because the cheaper untested options are unlikely to beat the current best.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000 with transformer aggregation (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). Every multimodal run scored between 0.48 and 0.53 and cost 4.6 to 6.6 GPU hours, so adding images has consistently hurt. Among RNA encoders, pca_n2000 beat scvi_n200 (0.619), which beat scgpt (0.328). Multiprofile clearly beat singleprofile (0.519). 2) Test: config_050 is RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200 with avgpool aggregation. It checks whether the transformer-over-avgpool advantage seen with PCA (0.713 vs 0.678) also holds for the second-best encoder. This tells us whether aggregation interacts with encoder choice. 3) Why this run: with one experiment left after this one, the expensive multimodal options are unlikely to beat 0.713 given four consistent failures. The only untested RNA-only multiprofile options are config_050 and config_051 (scgpt, avgpool). I chose config_050 because scvi_n200 was far stronger than scgpt. Even so, I do not expect it to exceed 0.713 (scvi with the transformer only reached 0.619), so its main value is the aggregation check rather than a new best. It is cheap at about 0.4 to 0.6 GPU hours, roughly a tenth of a multimodal run, which keeps total GPU hours low while 0.713 remains our best result.

1) Evidence: the best result is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 with a transformer aggregator (config_040, 0.713 acc / 0.695 F1). Every multimodal run scored between 0.48 and 0.53, whatever the fusion or image encoder, so adding images consistently hurts by about 0.18. That gap is unlikely to close by switching to weighted fusion or avgpool, since avgpool was worse than the transformer even for RNA-only. scGPT was clearly weak (0.33). Single-profile setups trail multiprofile by about 0.19 for PCA (0.519 vs 0.713). 2) Test: this run checks whether the single-profile penalty also holds for scVI. It completes the profile-setting comparison across RNA encoders and confirms that multiprofile aggregation is the key design choice. 3) Rationale: no remaining configuration has a realistic chance of beating 0.713. An expensive multimodal run (about 5–7 GPU hours) would very likely land near 0.5 and waste compute. This single-profile RNA-only run is the cheapest option, expected at about 0.05 GPU hours (similar to config_016's 0.04), so the budget ends with minimal extra GPU time. config_040 is expected to remain the best configuration.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet. Priors suggest that combining RNA and image data, aggregating over multiple profiles and using a learned transformer aggregator should give the highest accuracy, but this is untested. 2) config_007 tests that design: multimodal, multiprofile, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion. It pairs them with a compact scVI (200-dim) RNA encoder and a ResNet50 image encoder. That makes it a strong anchor for later comparisons: single-profile vs multiprofile, RNA-only vs multimodal, avgpool vs transformer, concat vs weighted, and scGPT/PCA vs scVI and ViT-L vs ResNet50. 3) It is a likely high performer and a good base for one-factor-at-a-time comparisons. It avoids the cost of ViT-L features until we know whether a larger image encoder is needed. Expected relative cost is moderate to high: multiprofile transformer aggregation over two modalities costs more than single-profile or unimodal runs. It should still be clearly cheaper than the equivalent ViT-L configurations (e.g., config_034).

Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_007 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1 at 6.22 GPU hours. We do not yet know which design choices drive that result. Test: config_010 changes only the aggregation, from transformer to avgpool, and keeps everything else fixed. This isolates whether the more expensive transformer aggregation actually improves accuracy. Why now: aggregation applies to every multiprofile configuration, so the answer shapes most of the remaining search. If avgpool matches 007, later RNA and image encoder comparisons (scGPT, ViT-L) can run in the cheaper avgpool space. If it is clearly worse, we keep transformer aggregation and stop spending on avgpool variants. Expected cost: somewhat below config_007's 6.22 GPU hours, since mean pooling is lighter than a transformer aggregator.

1. Evidence: The two experiments differ only in aggregation. With scVI + ResNet50 + weighted fusion, transformer reached 0.688 accuracy while avgpool reached 0.427. That is a large and consistent gap, and F1 agrees, so transformer aggregation is a strong working choice. The RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion type are still untested. 2. Test: This experiment keeps the best setup (multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer, weighted fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT. Because it is a single-variable change, any difference can be credited to the RNA representation, which is a major design choice for this task. 3. Why now: It builds on the best result so far while reducing uncertainty in a dimension that could plausibly raise accuracy. It also avoids the larger ViT-L image encoder until the RNA side is better understood. Expected cost is similar to config_007, about 6 to 7 GPU hours, possibly slightly more for scGPT embeddings. That is cheaper than the ViT-L variants.

1) Evidence: config_007 (scVI + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) is the clear leader at 0.688 acc / 0.659 F1. Swapping transformer for avgpool dropped it to 0.427, and swapping scVI for scGPT dropped it to 0.332. Both gaps are large, so transformer aggregation and scVI look like strong choices. The image encoder is the major design dimension that has not been tested at all; every run so far used ResNet50. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup and changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. That isolates whether richer image features add accuracy on top of the current best. 3) Fusion type (concat vs weighted) and PCA vs scVI are likely smaller refinements that can be checked later. The image encoder could shift accuracy substantially, and the answer decides which backbone the remaining 6 experiments should build on. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_007's 6.22 GPU hours, perhaps about 8–10 GPU hours, because ViT-L is a larger model. That is still cheaper than the 12.31 h scGPT run, and the potential gain justifies it.

1) Evidence: config_007 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted fusion) is clearly best at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. Each single-factor change away from it hurt badly. Swapping aggregation to avgpool gave 0.427, swapping RNA encoder to scgpt gave 0.332, and swapping image encoder to ViT-L gave 0.421. So the scvi, resnet50 and transformer choices look well supported. Fusion type is the one design axis next to the best config that has not been tested. 2) Test: config_012 changes only fusion, from weighted to concat, which isolates whether fusion strategy can improve on the current best. 3) Why now: this is a one-factor step from the leader, so it is the most direct way to find an improvement while also settling a design question. Testing pca_n2000 or other options can wait for later experiments. Expected cost is similar to config_007, about 6 GPU hours, because the architecture is the same apart from the fusion head. That is moderate, cheaper than the scgpt runs, and justified given how strong this region of the search space looks.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_007 (scVI + ResNet50 + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). One-factor comparisons point consistently the same way. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool by a wide margin (0.688 vs 0.427). ResNet50 beats ViT-L (0.688 vs 0.421). scVI beats scGPT (0.688 vs 0.332). Weighted fusion edges out concat (0.688 vs 0.650), with F1 agreeing. The main untested RNA encoder is pca_n2000. 2) Test: config_016 keeps the winning setup (ResNet50, transformer, weighted fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This isolates whether a simpler, higher-dimensional RNA representation can match or beat scVI. 3) Why now: it is the last unexplored design axis that could plausibly beat the current best, and it stays close to the strongest known configuration. That balances exploitation and exploration with 4 experiments left. Expected cost: moderate, roughly 6–7 GPU hours, similar to config_007 and well below scGPT's 12.3 hours.

1. Evidence: Within multiprofile multimodal models, config_007 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted, 0.688 accuracy) is best. Aggregation matters most: avgpool falls to 0.427. resnet50 clearly beats imagenet_vit_l (0.421). scvi_n200 beats pca_n2000 (0.629), which beats scgpt (0.332). Weighted fusion edges out concat (0.650), and F1 follows the same ordering. The main open question is the profile setting: every run so far was multiprofile. 2. Test: config_011 keeps the best encoder pair (scvi_n200 + resnet50) and weighted fusion but uses a single profile. This shows whether multiprofile aggregation is truly needed. The sharp avgpool drop suggests naive pooling across profiles can hurt, so single-profile modelling could plausibly match or beat the transformer. 3. Why now: This changes one variable from the current best, so the result will be easy to interpret. It resolves the last major untested design axis before the final 2 experiments are spent exploiting. Expected cost is low, likely below the roughly 6 GPU hours of the multiprofile transformer runs, since it needs no multiprofile aggregation.

1) Evidence: config_007 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, transformer, weighted fusion; 0.688 acc, 0.659 F1) is the best so far. Single-factor changes from it all scored lower. Avgpool (0.427), scGPT (0.332), ViT-L (0.421) and single-profile (0.525) were much worse. Concat (0.650) and PCA (0.629) were only slightly worse. The main open question is whether the image branch truly adds value. Weighted fusion beating concat, and the poor ViT-L result, both hint that the image signal may be noisy and partly down-weighted. 2) Test: config_004 keeps the winning RNA path (scVI, multiprofile, transformer) but drops the image modality. This isolates the image branch's contribution. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.688, it becomes a cheaper, possibly better optimum. If it falls short, that confirms multimodal fusion is needed, and the final experiment can refine around config_007. 3) Why now: the remaining near-neighbour variants (for example PCA+concat) combine two changes that each underperformed, so they are unlikely to beat config_007. This ablation answers an important untested design question. Expected cost is lower than config_007's 6.2 GPU hours, likely about 3–5 GPU hours, because there is no image encoder or fusion.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_007 (scVI + ResNet50 + transformer + weighted, 0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). Every single-factor change from it lowered accuracy. Swapping the RNA encoder to scGPT gave 0.33 and to PCA gave 0.63. Swapping the image encoder to ViT-L gave 0.42. Using avgpool instead of the transformer gave 0.43, concat fusion gave 0.65, and single-profile gave 0.53. RNA-only with the same scVI/transformer pipeline reached only 0.42, which suggests most of the signal comes from the ResNet50 image branch. The main untested design choice in this winning pipeline is the image-only arm, and its contribution is unknown. 2) This experiment tests image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile transformer aggregation. It shows how much of the 0.688 the image branch carries alone. If scVI fusion adds less than expected, or if the RNA branch adds noise, image-only could match or beat 0.688. Combinations of two already-worse changes, such as config_033 (PCA + concat), are unlikely to beat 0.688. 3) It reuses the proven ResNet50 + transformer components and has some chance of improving on the best result. It also clarifies modality contributions, which will guide the final experiment. Expected cost is low to moderate: it drops the RNA branch, so it should be cheaper than the roughly 6 GPU-hour multimodal transformer runs.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_007 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted, val acc 0.688, F1 0.659). The transformer aggregation, resnet50 and multimodal setting are each clearly important. Avgpool dropped accuracy to 0.43, imagenet_vit_l to 0.42, scGPT to 0.33, and single-profile to 0.53. Within this strong region, pca_n2000 with weighted fusion scored 0.629, and concat fusion with scvi scored 0.650. The one untested combination in this backbone is pca_n2000 with concat fusion. 2) Test: whether pca_n2000 pairs better with concat fusion than with weighted fusion, which would mean the two factors interact. This matters because the higher-dimensional PCA input might benefit from direct concatenation. 3) Why this choice: it is the last experiment and only the best accuracy counts, so I am spending it on the one untested option inside the clearly dominant resnet50 + transformer region. Every alternative changes a factor that has already shown large drops. Admittedly, the additive evidence suggests it will likely land around 0.60-0.65, and config_007 will probably remain the final best. Expected cost is moderate, about 5-7 GPU hours, similar to config_012 and config_016.

1) Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so we have no data on modality, profile setting, encoders, aggregation or fusion. Domain priors suggest that combining RNA and image modalities and aggregating several profiles per sample usually improve accuracy. 2) What it tests: config_019 is a strong, mid-complexity anchor (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 RNA encoder, resnet50 image encoder, simple avgpool aggregation, concat fusion). It checks whether the multimodal multiprofile direction is as promising as expected. It uses the simplest and cheapest component choices, so later runs can vary one factor at a time: a ViT-L image encoder, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, or a different RNA encoder like scGPT or PCA. It also lets us ablate down to single-modality or single-profile variants to confirm each component helps. 3) Why now: a likely high-performing but not maximally expensive starting point gives a solid incumbent early and a clean reference for factor-wise comparisons within the 10-run budget. Expected cost is moderate. Multiprofile aggregation and two modalities add cost over single-modality or single-profile runs, but resnet50 and avgpool keep it well below ViT-L and transformer variants.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI RNA encoder, ResNet50 images, avgpool, concat) reached 0.411 accuracy and 0.378 F1 for 7.27 GPU hours. One run cannot tell us which design choices drive performance, and the image encoder is one of the biggest open questions. 2) Test: config_008 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else fixed. That makes it a clean comparison of how much a stronger image representation helps inside the same multimodal, multiprofile setup. 3) Why now: the image backbone is likely to have a large effect on accuracy. If ViT-L clearly wins, it becomes the base for later tests of transformer aggregation, weighted fusion and alternative RNA encoders. If it does not, we can stay with the cheaper ResNet50 for the rest of the budget. Expected cost is higher than config_019, roughly 1.5–2x (about 11–15 GPU hours), because ViT-L is a larger model. That cost is justified because this choice could plausibly hold the best configuration.

1) Evidence: The two runs differ only in the image encoder. Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L, with the same multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, avgpool and concat setup, raised validation accuracy from 0.411 to 0.514 and F1 from 0.378 to 0.498. It also cut cost from 7.27 to 4.49 GPU hours, so ViT-L is the clear image encoder to build on. The biggest untested design choice in this strong setting is the aggregation method: transformer versus avgpool. 2) Test: config_025 keeps the best config_008 setup and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles adds accuracy over simple pooling. 3) Why now: This one-variable extension of the current best is the most likely to beat it, and the result will decide aggregation for all later multiprofile runs. RNA encoder and fusion type can be tested afterwards. Expected cost is moderate, somewhat above config_008's 4.49 GPU hours because of the transformer aggregator, likely about 5 to 6 GPU hours, and still below the ResNet50 run.

1) Evidence: with scVI RNA features and concat fusion held fixed, the ViT-L image encoder beat ResNet50 (0.514 vs 0.411). Switching ViT-L from avgpool to transformer aggregation gave a large further gain (0.678 accuracy, F1 0.646, config_025). The image encoder and aggregation choices look settled. The RNA encoder is completely unexplored: every run so far used scvi_n200. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, concat) and swaps only scvi_n200 for scGPT. That isolates whether a richer foundation-model RNA embedding adds signal on top of the strongest pipeline. 3) Of the remaining single-factor choices, RNA encoder is plausibly larger in effect than fusion type (concat vs weighted), so it is the most informative next step. If it wins, it becomes the new base for testing fusion; if not, scVI is confirmed and the remaining budget can go to fusion or pca_n2000. Expected cost is similar to or slightly above config_025 (about 4.7–5.5 GPU hours), because scGPT embeddings are somewhat larger than scVI's 200 dimensions.

1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation gave the largest gain so far, from 0.514 (avgpool, config_008) to 0.678 (config_025, scvi_n200 + ViT-L + transformer + concat). ViT-L clearly beat ResNet50. scVI clearly beat scGPT under the transformer setup (0.678 vs 0.540). Fusion is the main design choice not yet tested: every run so far used concat. 2) Test: config_041 keeps the best setup and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This cleanly shows whether learned modality weighting adds accuracy and F1 on top of the current best, and which fusion to use for the remaining runs, such as later testing pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder. 3) Why now: it exploits the strongest direction while answering an open, important question with a single change. Expected cost is similar to config_025, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, since weighted fusion adds little overhead. That makes it a moderate-cost, high-value next step.

1. Evidence: Multiprofile multimodal runs with a ViT-L image encoder and transformer aggregation are the strongest so far. config_025 (scVI RNA encoder, concat fusion) is best at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Changing one component of config_025 hurt each time: scGPT dropped to 0.540, weighted fusion to 0.591, avgpool aggregation to 0.514, and ResNet50 avgpool reached only 0.411. The RNA encoder clearly matters, and the third option, PCA with 2000 components, is still untested. 2. Test: config_030 keeps the best setup (ViT-L, transformer, concat) and swaps scVI for PCA-2000. This shows whether a simpler, higher-dimensional RNA representation can beat scVI. 3. Why now: Swapping the RNA encoder has produced the largest swings seen so far, so this is the most likely single change to raise the best accuracy. It is also a direct exploit of the top configuration. Expected cost is similar to config_025, roughly 4–5 GPU hours, possibly slightly more from the larger PCA input. That is well below the ResNet50 runs.

1) Evidence: config_025 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) is clearly best at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Each single-factor change from it lowered accuracy: scGPT gave 0.540, PCA gave 0.520, weighted fusion gave 0.591, and avgpool aggregation gave 0.514. ResNet50 was also worse than ViT-L under avgpool (0.411 vs 0.514). The local neighborhood around config_025 is now well mapped. The main open question is how much the RNA branch actually contributes. The RNA encoder choice swung accuracy by about 0.15, which could mean scVI adds a lot or that weaker RNA embeddings add noise. 2) This experiment: config_024 is the image-only version of the winning recipe (multiprofile ViT-L with transformer aggregation). It directly tests whether RNA fusion helps. If it scores near or above 0.678, the remaining budget should go to image-centric variants. If it scores well below, multimodal scVI fusion is confirmed as essential and later runs should refine around config_025. 3) Why now: the remaining multimodal neighbors (e.g., ResNet50 with transformer) are unlikely to win given the ResNet result. This ablation resolves the largest structural uncertainty and also has some chance of matching the current best. Expected cost: lower than the multimodal runs, roughly 3–4 GPU hours, since there is no RNA encoder or fusion step.

1) Evidence: config_025 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) is clearly best at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Most single-factor changes from it hurt. Switching to scGPT or PCA RNA encoders dropped accuracy to 0.52–0.54. Weighted fusion dropped it to 0.59. ResNet50 was much weaker than ViT-L under avgpool (0.41 vs 0.51). Image-only with transformer reached only 0.507, so the scVI RNA branch carries much of the signal. The main open question near the optimum is whether the image branch truly helps on top of scVI, or whether scVI alone with transformer aggregation is as good or better. 2) This experiment runs RNA-only, scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer aggregation. That isolates the RNA contribution and shows whether the ~0.17 gain over image-only comes from fusion or mainly from scVI. If it matches or beats 0.678, it is a cheaper and possibly better optimum. If it falls short, that confirms multimodal fusion and points the last experiment at remaining multimodal neighbours such as config_023 or config_006. 3) It is the most informative untested neighbour of the best configuration. The ResNet50 variant is unlikely to win given the prior ResNet result. Expected cost is low, about 1–2 GPU hours, similar to the image-only run and well below the ~4.6 h multimodal runs.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with transformer aggregation over multiple profiles (config_010, acc 0.715, F1 0.687). It beats every multimodal run, and adding images consistently lowered accuracy. Within multimodal runs, scVI clearly beat scGPT and PCA, and transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool. So the RNA encoder and aggregation choices look settled. The profile setting has never been tested: every experiment so far was multiprofile. 2. Test: config_004 is RNA-only scVI with a single profile. It isolates whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed for the strongest modality, or whether the simpler single-profile model matches or beats 0.715. 3. Why now: the other RNA-only options (scGPT or PCA encoders, avgpool aggregation) change choices that already lost clearly, so they are unlikely to beat config_010. Profile setting is the one major design axis with zero evidence, so this run reduces the most uncertainty. It also leaves the last experiment free to exploit whichever profile setting wins. Expected cost is the lowest of any option, below config_010's 0.40 GPU hours, since there is no aggregation and no image branch.

Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile scVI with transformer aggregation (config_010, 0.715 acc / 0.687 F1). That beats every multimodal variant, including the best one (config_025, 0.678). So image fusion has not helped. Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.678 vs 0.514), which makes config_009 unlikely to win. ResNet50 underperformed ViT-L, so config_023 is unlikely to win either. The remaining open question is whether another RNA encoder can beat scVI in the RNA-only transformer setting. In multimodal runs scGPT and PCA trailed scVI, but those runs included the image branch, which may have masked RNA-encoder differences. Between the two, scGPT edged out PCA (0.540 vs 0.520 acc; 0.524 vs 0.479 F1). This final experiment tests RNA-only multiprofile scGPT with transformer aggregation, the most plausible untested route to exceeding 0.715. The chance of beating config_010 is modest, but it is the best remaining shot. Expected cost is very low (about 0.4–0.6 GPU hours, comparable to config_010), far cheaper than any multimodal option.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence about any design choice yet. Priors suggest that combining both modalities and aggregating over multiple profiles should give the highest accuracy for cellular profiling. 2) Config_013 tests that prior directly: it is multimodal and multiprofile, uses transformer aggregation and concat fusion, and pairs a compact RNA encoder (scVI, 200 dimensions) with a mid-sized image encoder (ResNet50). It gives a strong anchor result. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time: the image encoder (ViT-L), the RNA encoder (PCA or scGPT), the aggregation method (avgpool) and the fusion method (weighted). Simpler baselines such as single-modality or single-profile runs can be checked later if needed. 3) Starting near the expected best region, but with cheaper components than scGPT or ViT-L, balances getting a high result early against compute cost. Expected relative cost is medium. Multiprofile transformer aggregation and multimodal processing add training time, but the small scVI and ResNet50 representations keep it below the ViT-L and scGPT variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have one result so far. config_013 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI RNA encoder, ResNet50 images, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.427 accuracy and 0.417 F1. One run says nothing yet about which design choices matter most. The image encoder is plausibly a major lever, since ImageNet ViT-L gives much richer image features than ResNet50. 2. What this tests: config_003 changes only the image encoder (ResNet50 to ViT-L) and keeps everything else the same. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the image backbone. This settles a key design choice that splits about half of the remaining search space. 3. Why it is the best next step: The image encoder is likely the largest source of accuracy gain, and testing it now tells us which backbone to carry into later RNA-encoder, aggregation and fusion comparisons. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_013, roughly 1.3–1.6x (about 7–8 GPU hours), because ViT-L embeddings are larger. That cost is justified because it may well be the stronger backbone. If ViT-L shows no gain, we can switch to cheaper ResNet50 variants for the rest of the search.

1) Evidence: with the scVI RNA encoder, multiprofile transformer aggregation and concat fusion held fixed, the ViT-L image encoder beat ResNet50 by a clear margin (acc 0.485 vs 0.427, F1 0.464 vs 0.417). ViT-L was also slightly cheaper (4.65 vs 5.16 GPU h). So ViT-L should be the image backbone going forward. The RNA encoder choice is still completely untested, and it is likely a major driver of accuracy. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer, concat) and swaps scVI for scGPT. It isolates the effect of a pretrained foundation-model RNA embedding against scVI. 3) Choosing the RNA encoder is the biggest open design question. Settling it early lets the remaining 7 experiments fine-tune fusion (weighted vs concat) and aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) around the best encoder pair. 1. Evidence: The RNA encoder is the largest lever so far. Swapping scVI for scGPT, with ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fusion, raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.632, and F1 rose in step (0.464 to 0.607). ViT-L also beat ResNet50 under scVI. The main uncertainty is fusion: every run so far used concat, so weighted fusion is completely untested. 2. Test: config_019 keeps the best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT, ViT-L, transformer) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This cleanly measures whether weighting the modalities improves on the current best, which matters because scGPT RNA features may deserve more weight than the image features. 3. Why now: It exploits the strongest region found so far while resolving a design choice that has had no exploration. Any gain directly raises the best accuracy, and the result guides the remaining 6 runs. Those runs can then test pca_n2000 RNA (config_007/029) and avgpool aggregation. Expected cost is similar to config_001, about 4 GPU hours, since weighted fusion adds negligible overhead to the multiprofile transformer pipeline.

1) Evidence: scGPT with ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fusion (config_001) is clearly best at 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. scGPT beat scVI by about 0.15 under the same setup. ViT-L beat ResNet50 for scVI. Weighted fusion did worse than concat (0.591). Aggregation has never been varied: every run so far used a transformer, so it is the largest untested design choice around the best setup. 2) This experiment keeps the best RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion fixed and swaps transformer aggregation for avgpool. That isolates whether the transformer aggregator is needed or whether simpler pooling matches or beats it. 3) Of the untested choices, this one is most likely to produce a new best, and it settles a choice that decides how the remaining 5 experiments should be spent. Expected cost is low to moderate: avgpool should train somewhat faster than the transformer runs (about 3–4 GPU hours, below config_001's 3.95).

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_001 (scGPT + ViT-L + transformer + concat, 0.632 accuracy, 0.607 F1). Within that setup, weighted fusion (0.591) and avgpool aggregation (0.523) both did worse. Switching the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT gave the largest gain seen (+0.15). That makes the RNA encoder the most influential choice. Its third option, pca_n2000, has not been tested in any context. 2) Test: config_007 keeps the best context (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, concat) and swaps scGPT for PCA-2000. This shows whether PCA features beat or match scGPT. If PCA wins, the best result improves directly. If it loses, scGPT is confirmed and the remaining 3 experiments can target other questions, such as single-profile or RNA-only variants. 3) Why now: This experiment completes the most impactful design axis in the most promising context, so it is the best balance of exploration and exploitation. Expected cost is moderate, about 4–5 GPU hours, similar to config_001 and config_003, since the transformer aggregation is the same and PCA features are cheap.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder matters most so far. With ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fusion, scGPT scored 0.632, against 0.514 for PCA and 0.485 for scVI. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.632 vs 0.523), and concat beat weighted fusion (0.632 vs 0.591). ViT-L beat ResNet50 in the scVI pairing (0.485 vs 0.427), so a ResNet50 swap is unlikely to win. The open question is whether the image branch adds signal at all, since no unimodal run has been done. 2) Test: config_017 keeps the best settings (scGPT, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) but drops images. This isolates how much the image modality contributes. If it matches or beats 0.632, the image branch is noise and the best model is simpler. If it falls well short, multimodal fusion is confirmed and the last runs can focus on refining around config_001. 3) Why now: It is both a real chance at a new best and a direct test of an untested design choice, at low cost. Removing the ViT-L image pathway should make it cheaper than config_001's 3.95 GPU hours, likely around 2–3.

Evidence: the RNA-only model (scGPT, multiprofile, transformer, config_017) is the best result so far at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. It was also the cheapest run at 0.51 GPU hours. Every multimodal variant did worse (at most 0.632), which suggests the image branch adds noise. Within multimodal runs, scGPT clearly beat scVI and PCA as the RNA encoder, and transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 0.11. So swapping the encoder or switching to avgpool is unlikely to beat 0.721. Uncertainty: the profile setting has never been tested, since every run so far used multiprofile. This experiment tests whether single-profile scGPT RNA-only can match or beat multiprofile aggregation. That is the main untested design choice left in the most promising model family. Budget: with 2 experiments remaining after this one, the result tells us whether to refine further around multiprofile RNA-only or around single-profile RNA-only. Expected cost: very low, likely below config_017's 0.51 GPU hours because there is no aggregation step and no image processing. It should be among the cheapest options available.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_017 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scGPT, transformer) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Adding images has hurt in every multimodal run, with a best of 0.632. scGPT is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, ahead of PCA (0.514) and scVI (0.485) in matched multimodal comparisons. Multiprofile beats singleprofile for scGPT RNA-only (0.721 vs 0.650). 2) Question: Aggregation is the only design choice for the leading configuration not yet tested in the RNA-only setting. Avgpool did worse than the transformer in the multimodal setting (0.523 vs 0.632). However, a simpler pooling head could behave differently, and possibly overfit less, on a lower-dimensional RNA-only input. config_032 tests scGPT RNA-only multiprofile with avgpool. 3) Why this experiment: The other plausible candidates, scVI or PCA RNA-only multiprofile, swap in encoders that were consistently much weaker than scGPT. They are unlikely to beat 0.721. This run keeps the strongest components and varies the one remaining open choice, so it offers the best chance of improving on the current best with 2 experiments left. Expected cost is very low, around 0.3–0.6 GPU hours, similar to config_017 and far cheaper than any multimodal run.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scGPT with transformer aggregation (config_017, acc 0.721, F1 0.681). Adding the image branch consistently lowered accuracy (best multimodal 0.632). Transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool, both in the multimodal runs and in the RNA-only runs. Among RNA encoders in the multimodal setting, scGPT led, PCA-2000 came second (0.514) and scVI came last (0.485). No other scGPT RNA-only configuration remains untested. 2. Test: config_008 keeps the winning RNA-only + multiprofile + transformer recipe and swaps in PCA-2000, the second-best encoder. It checks whether the encoder ranking seen in multimodal runs also holds without image noise. It is the most plausible remaining path to beating 0.721, because image-only and multimodal options have shown no sign of exceeding RNA-only. 3. Why now: As the final experiment, it is the logical exploitation of the strongest design pattern found. It is also very cheap: RNA-only multiprofile runs cost about 0.4–0.5 GPU hours, roughly a tenth of a multimodal run, so the low cost justifies the modest chance of a gain.

1) Evidence: no experiments have been run, so every design choice is uncertain. Priors from multimodal cellular profiling suggest three things: combining RNA and image modalities usually beats either one alone, aggregating multiple profiles usually beats single profiles, and stronger image encoders (ViT-L) and compact learned RNA embeddings (scVI) often do well. 2) Test: config_013 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) sets a strong 'everything likely-good' anchor. It tells us early what accuracy ceiling is realistic. Later experiments can then ablate one factor at a time from this anchor (avgpool vs transformer, resnet50 vs ViT-L, scGPT/PCA vs scVI, weighted vs concat, unimodal baselines) to see which components actually matter and which can be swapped for cheaper options. 3) Why now: only the best accuracy counts, so getting a likely top performer early protects the result and gives a reference for judging cheaper variants. Expected cost: relatively high, among the more expensive options because it combines multiprofile transformer aggregation, multimodal processing and ViT-L features. It should still be cheaper than PCA-2000 variants because the scVI representation is compact. Later experiments will favour cheaper ablations.

With a single data point, we don't yet know which design choices drive performance. 2. This experiment changes only the aggregation, swapping the transformer for avgpool, and keeps everything else fixed. A one-factor change gives a clean comparison against the current best, and the answer guides many later multiprofile picks (encoder and fusion variants). 1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_013 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1. Test: config_037 keeps everything in config_013 the same and switches only the fusion from concat to weighted. This isolates the effect of fusion and may improve on the best result. 3. 1) Evidence: single-profile multimodal config_002 (scVI + ViT-L, concat) reached 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1 for only 0.62 GPU h. That beats every multi-profile run (0.52-0.59) by about 9 points, which suggests the multi-profile aggregation setup is a weak direction. 1. Evidence: Singleprofile multimodal (config_002: scVI + ViT-L, concat) is clearly the best result at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1, and it cost only 0.62 GPU hours. Every multiprofile variant scored 0.52-0.59 while costing 3.6-5.2 GPU hours. Within multiprofile, the earlier runs consistently favored scVI over scGPT or PCA, ViT-L over ResNet50, and concat over weighted fusion. RNA-only singleprofile (config_048) was weak at 0.328. That suggests the image branch carries most of the signal. The key untested question is whether the RNA branch helps or adds noise in the singleprofile setting.
2. Test: Image-only singleprofile with ViT-L isolates the image contribution. It could exceed config_002 if RNA is diluting the signal. If it scores lower, that confirms multimodal fusion helps, and the final experiment can refine the singleprofile multimodal setup (for example fusion type or RNA encoder).
3. Why now: It is the cheapest informative experiment, expected to cost about 0.5 GPU hours, similar to or slightly less than config_002 and roughly 8-10x cheaper than any multiprofile run. It has a realistic chance of a new best, and its result directly guides the last experiment.

1. Evidence: Single-profile multimodal with scVI and ViT-L using concat fusion (config_002) is clearly the best so far, at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1, for only 0.62 GPU hours. Every multiprofile variant scored much lower, at 0.52-0.59, and cost 4-5 GPU hours each. Within the multiprofile runs, each single change from the best setup lowered accuracy: weighted fusion by about 0.05, scGPT by about 0.06, PCA by about 0.07 (with the worst F1), and ResNet50 by about 0.07. Weighted fusion kept the highest F1 among those variants, so it is the least damaging known change. Fusion type has also never been tested in the single-profile setting, where the balance between modalities may play out differently than under aggregation. 2. Test: this run keeps the best single-profile setup (scVI, ViT-L) and swaps concat for weighted fusion. It checks whether learned modality weighting can beat concatenation when profiles are not aggregated. 3. Why: with only this last experiment left, the best chance of beating 0.678 is the closest neighbour of the best configuration that carries the least prior evidence of harm.
