1) There is no history yet, so all design choices are uncertain. Priors from multimodal profiling suggest that combining RNA and image, aggregating across multiple profiles, and using stronger encoders tend to give the highest accuracy, but none of this has been tested here. 2) config_024 combines several of these choices: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI RNA embeddings, ImageNet ViT-L image features, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion. It tests whether this high-capacity combination works well on this data. It also sets a strong reference point that later, cheaper ablations (avgpool aggregation, ResNet50, unimodal or single-profile settings) can be compared against. 3) Since only the best accuracy counts, establishing a likely-strong configuration early is a reasonable use of the first slot, and the 9 remaining experiments leave room for cost-saving ablations. I chose scVI's compact 200-dimensional embedding over scGPT and PCA-2000 to limit input size and cost while keeping a learned representation. Expected relative cost: high. Multiprofile transformer aggregation, ViT-L features and multimodal fusion make it among the most expensive options, though somewhat cheaper than the scGPT variants.

Evidence: there is only one result so far. The full multimodal, multiprofile model (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.527 accuracy and 0.510 F1 at 3.6 GPU hours. Evidence: with scVI + ViT-L + weighted fusion, the single-profile model (0.540 acc, 0.524 F1, 0.53 GPU h) slightly beat the multi-profile transformer (0.527 acc, 3.60 GPU h) at about one-seventh the cost. 1. Evidence: the best result so far is the cheap singleprofile scvi_n200 + ViT-L model with weighted fusion (config_027, acc 0.540, F1 0.524, 0.53 GPU h). The multiprofile transformer version (config_024) scored lower (0.527) and cost about 7x more. Swapping scvi for scgpt also hurt (0.525, with lower F1). 1. Evidence: weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.540 vs 0.422 with the same other settings). Singleprofile scvi_n200 + ViT-L + weighted (config_027, 0.540) is the current best. The multiprofile transformer version scored slightly lower (0.527) at about 7x the cost. scvi_n200 edges out scgpt (0.540 vs 0.525, with higher F1), but the third RNA encoder, pca_n2000, is untested. 2. Test: config_008 keeps the best cheap setup (singleprofile, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and swaps in pca_n2000. 1. Evidence: Weighted fusion is clearly better than concat (0.540 vs 0.422 with scvi_n200 and ViT-L). With weighted fusion, the RNA encoders differ only slightly (scvi 0.540 > pca 0.535 > scgpt 0.525), so scvi_n200 + ViT-L + weighted is the strongest base. Multiprofile has been tried only once, with transformer aggregation (0.527 accuracy, 3.6 GPU h). That run underperformed singleprofile and was about 7x more expensive. One run is too little to rule out multiprofile: the transformer aggregator may simply be overfitting or hard to optimise, while avgpool is a simpler, more robust way to aggregate profiles. 2. Test: config_019 keeps the best components (scvi_n200, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and swaps only the aggregator to avgpool. This isolates whether multiprofile aggregation can beat the 0.540 singleprofile result. 3. Why now: Aggregation is the main remaining design choice that could give a substantial accuracy gain, whereas the RNA encoder looks nearly saturated. Resolving it now leaves 3 runs to exploit the answer, for example trying pca_n2000 with avgpool or testing a ResNet50 image encoder cheaply in singleprofile. Expected cost is moderate to high, likely about 2-3 GPU h. 1. Evidence: weighted fusion clearly beats concat (about 0.54 vs 0.42). Singleprofile matches or beats multiprofile (0.540 vs 0.527 for transformer and 0.520 for avgpool) while costing 5 to 9 times fewer GPU hours. Among RNA encoders, scvi_n200 (0.540) and pca_n2000 (0.535) are about equal and both ahead of scgpt (0.525). The image encoder has never been varied, because every run so far used imagenet_vit_l. 2. Possible outcomes: if resnet50 matches or beats ViT-L, it could become the new best. If it is worse, it confirms ViT-L and points the remaining two experiments toward exploiting the singleprofile ViT-L weighted configurations. Expected cost is low, about 0.5 GPU hours, similar to or below config_027, since resnet50 features are smaller than ViT-L. That makes it a cheap, informative test compared with the 3.6 to 4.8 GPU-hour multiprofile runs.

Evidence: switching the image encoder from ViT-L to ResNet50 in the best single-profile scVI + weighted-fusion setup gave the largest gain so far (0.540 to 0.629 accuracy, F1 0.599). Other choices barely mattered. RNA encoders differed only slightly with ViT-L (scVI 0.540, PCA 0.535, scGPT 0.525). Multiprofile aggregation did not help (0.520 to 0.527) and cost 6 to 9 times more GPU hours. Concat fusion clearly hurt (0.422). Open question: is the gain driven entirely by ResNet50 image features, with RNA adding little or even noise? This test: the single-profile, image-only ResNet50 model (config_028) isolates the image contribution. If it matches or beats 0.629, the last experiment should go to image-only variants. If it falls short, RNA fusion is confirmed useful and the last run can refine the RNA encoder or try a ResNet50 multiprofile model. Why now: swapping the RNA encoder is unlikely to beat scVI, and multiprofile runs are costly with no demonstrated benefit. This answers a key design question and could itself produce the best model. Expected cost: lowest of the options, probably about 0.4 to 0.5 GPU hours, slightly below the 0.59 h of config_029 since there is no RNA branch.

1. Evidence: Switching the image encoder from ViT-L to ResNet50 gave the largest gain so far. config_029 (scVI + ResNet50, single-profile, weighted fusion) reached 0.629 accuracy and 0.599 F1, against about 0.54 for the ViT-L versions. Weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.540 vs 0.422). Multiprofile aggregation did not help with ViT-L (transformer 0.527, avgpool 0.520, vs 0.540 single-profile) and cost 6–9 times more GPU hours. Among RNA encoders, scVI (0.540) and PCA (0.535) were close, with scGPT lower (0.525). The remaining open question is whether another RNA encoder paired with ResNet50 can beat scVI. 2. Test: config_042 keeps the winning recipe (ResNet50, single-profile, weighted fusion) and swaps in PCA-2000. PCA was nearly tied with scVI under ViT-L. This tells us whether the ResNet50 gain carries over across RNA encoders and could give a new best. 3. Why now: This is a low-risk extension of the best configuration that could plausibly top 0.629. It is also cheap, about 0.6–0.8 GPU hours, similar to config_029/008. 1) Evidence: The clear leader is config_029 (scVI RNA + ResNet50 image, single profile, weighted fusion) at 0.629 accuracy and 0.599 F1. Swapping ResNet50 in for ViT-L gave a large gain (+0.09). Weighted fusion beats concat by a wide margin (~0.12), so concat options are not worth testing. scGPT trailed scVI by about 0.015 with ViT-L, which argues against config_017. With ViT-L, multiprofile transformer aggregation (0.527) came close to single profile (0.540) and beat avgpool (0.520). That aggregation choice has never been tried with the stronger ResNet50 backbone. 2) Test: config_031 keeps every winning choice (scVI, ResNet50, weighted fusion) and adds transformer aggregation over multiple profiles. 1) Evidence: no experiments have been completed, so the main uncertainties are whether multimodal fusion and multiprofile aggregation help, and how much the encoder choice matters. 2) Test: config_002 sets a strong but simple anchor. It combines multimodal inputs and multiprofile aggregation, the two choices most likely to lift accuracy, with the cheapest components: PCA-2000 RNA features, a ResNet50 image encoder, average pooling and concat fusion. Later runs can change one factor at a time from this point: transformer aggregation, ViT-L images, learned RNA encoders (scVI or scGPT), single-modality ablations or weighted fusion. 3) Why now: it should give a competitive accuracy early and a clean reference for the remaining 9 experiments. 1) Evidence and uncertainty: we have one result. The multimodal, multiprofile configuration (PCA RNA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.520 validation accuracy and 0.479 F1 at a high cost of 36.4 GPU hours. 1) Evidence: with everything else fixed (pca_n2000 + resnet50 + concat), the singleprofile setup (config_003) beat the multiprofile avgpool setup (config_002) on both accuracy (0.715 vs 0.520) and F1 (0.687 vs 0.479). 1) Evidence: the best result so far is single-profile multimodal with pca_n2000, ResNet50 and concat fusion (0.715 acc, 0.687 F1), at only 0.85 GPU h. 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_003 (single-profile, PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50, concat fusion) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_003 (singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Every single change away from it hurt. It only slightly beats the single-profile config_003 (0.715). 1) Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so there is no measured accuracy or cost to build on. Priors from multimodal cellular profiling suggest three things: combining RNA and image usually beats either modality alone, aggregating multiple profiles usually beats a single profile, and ViT-L image features are usually stronger than ResNet50. 2) What this tests: config_017 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA, ViT-L image, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) checks whether this likely-strong combination performs well. Simple avgpool and concat set a baseline, so later runs can measure whether transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, other RNA encoders, or unimodal and single-profile variants help or hurt. 3) Why now: with 9 runs left, starting at a likely-strong point lets later experiments both exploit gains and run informative ablations. Evidence: only one result exists so far. config_017 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.514 accuracy and 0.498 F1 at 4.49 GPU hours. Why now: if the transformer helps, later experiments can exploit it across encoder and fusion variants. If it does not help, we can stay with the cheaper avgpool. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_017, roughly 5–6 GPU hours, because of the attention-based aggregator. That cost is justified because this configuration has a good chance of becoming the best one.

1) Evidence: holding the scvi_n200 RNA encoder, ViT-L image encoder and concat fusion fixed, transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 7 points in accuracy (0.586 vs 0.514), with F1 agreeing (0.574 vs 0.498). That is the clearest signal so far, so transformer aggregation is the base to build on. 1) Evidence so far: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.586 vs 0.514 with scvi, vit_l, concat). Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.586 vs 0.514), and concat fusion beats weighted (0.586 vs 0.536). Switching the image encoder from ViT-L to ResNet50 gave the largest gain, raising the best result to 0.713 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + concat). 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_051 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + concat, 0.713 accuracy). Swapping ViT-L for ResNet50 gave a gain of about 0.11. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_051 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + concat) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1, well ahead of everything else. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.586 vs 0.514), and multiprofile with a strong RNA encoder is clearly favoured. The fusion choice is less settled. The only fusion comparison came from the weaker scVI + ViT-L context, where concat won (0.586 vs 0.536). Encoders also interact strongly: ResNet50 helped scGPT a lot but not scVI. 1) No experiments have been run yet, so I am relying only on priors. For cellular profiling, the strongest results usually come from combining RNA and image modalities and from aggregating multiple profiles per sample. That makes the multimodal multiprofile region the most likely place to find the best accuracy. 2) This experiment sets an anchor in that region using components I expect to be robust: compact scVI RNA embeddings (n=200), a strong ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, simple avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. Later runs can then each change one factor and compare against it: transformer vs. avgpool aggregation, weighted vs. concat fusion, other RNA encoders, ResNet50 vs. ViT-L, or unimodal and single-profile ablations. 3) This is likely the best opening use of the budget because it has a good chance of being near-optimal while staying cheaper than the full transformer-aggregation variants. 1. Evidence: Only one experiment has been run. config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.422 accuracy and 0.405 F1, which is a reasonable baseline. Aggregation is a key untested design choice. Average pooling treats all profiles in a set the same, while a transformer can learn which profiles matter and how they interact. 2. Test: config_049 keeps every other setting the same and swaps avgpool for transformer aggregation. This is a clean single-factor comparison, so any change in accuracy or F1 can be attributed to the aggregation method. 3. Why now: Aggregation could plausibly give large gains, and its answer shapes about half of the remaining search space, since many multiprofile configurations use one aggregator or the other. Settling it early guides how the remaining 8 experiments are spent. Expected cost is moderately higher than the 4.49 GPU-hour baseline, roughly 1.2–1.5x, because of the added transformer layers over the profile set. That is justified because this setting is a strong candidate for the best-performing configuration.

1) Evidence: Switching aggregation from avgpool to transformer raised validation accuracy from 0.42 to 0.71, with F1 rising alongside it. Everything else was held fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, ViT-L, concat). That is strong evidence that transformer aggregation over multiple profiles is the right backbone. The other design choices are still untested: RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion. 2) Test: Keep the winning setup and swap only the RNA encoder, scvi_n200 for scGPT. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation adds accuracy. 3) Rationale: The encoder is likely to matter more than the concat-vs-weighted fusion choice, so it is the most informative single change to exploit the strong direction. Later experiments can then test fusion (config_017/029) and a cheaper ResNet50 image encoder. Expected cost is similar to config_049, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, possibly slightly more because scGPT embeddings are larger.
